## D212 — Architecture policy: customization lives on the extension plane; durian-pi ships as two minimum products (operator ruling, 2026-11-05)

**Decision.** Three clauses, from the operator, and they are a **standing architecture policy**, not a feature:

1. **Any customization to durian-pi is served as an extension, not as code built into the base.** A change that cannot
   be expressed as an extension is evidence the base is missing an extension point — the base grows a *seam*, never a
   *feature*.
2. **Minimum product 1 — the base coding agent.** A minimum coding agent on top of `pi-durable` that "operates just
   fine without the extensions". It must boot, hold a conversation, edit files, run commands, keep its own durable
   history and recover from a crash with **zero durian-pi extensions loaded**.
3. **Minimum product 2 — durian-pi, the team.** A team of specialized agents that cooperate (roles, a durable queue,
   routing, review/verification, the landing path). It is *a consumer of* the base, sitting on the extension plane.

**Naming (proposed here, operator ratifies — precedent: the last rename was an operator decision, D103).** Pi's own
family names by role with a `pi-` prefix: `pi-ai`, `pi-agent-core`, `pi-coding-agent`, `pi-durable`, `pi-tui`,
`pi-web-ui` (all live in `package.json` dependencies). This project's derivative convention was set by D103:
`<name>-pi` for the product, `DURIAN_PI_*` for env, `<name>.config.json` for config — hence `durian-pi`. Following
that, the base agent is **`durian-core`** (mirrors `pi-agent-core`'s role: the thing you build a product *on*), and the
team product keeps the name **`durian-pi`**. Alternatives considered: `durian-agent` (mirrors `pi-coding-agent`, but
names the *role* not the *substrate*, and the team is also agents — ambiguous); `pi-durian` (reads as an upstream pi
family package, which it is not — this is downstream and depends on pi, misleading in the wrong direction);
`durian-base` (true but not a name). `durian-core` was recommended because the distinction the policy needs is
*substrate vs product*, which is exactly the `-core` distinction in the family this project already descends from.
A rename touches env (`DURIAN_PI_*` → two prefixes), config file names, and `package.json` — which today still reads
**`"name": "durig"`**, i.e. **D103's acceptance criterion (`git grep -i durig` returns only deliberate alias sites)
is not met**, measured 2026-11-05: `node -e "console.log(require('./package.json').name)"` → `durig`, and the
registered config vocabulary is still `DURIG_*` (`src/config.mjs` `CONFIG_KEYS`). That is a real open item for `pm`,
not a new idea — it belongs in the same row as the naming decision.

**The open design question, deliberately not decided.** Whether the team shares **one instance** of the base agent or
each member runs **its own instance with its own SQLite database** is a prior-art question. The operator declined to
guess; under the research-before-design ruling (D210) it goes to research first. Our own rig's current answer, measured
2026-11-05 (Linux Fedora 45 7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64 node v24.22.1) so the research compares against a real system:
**one broker process** supervising **12 seat processes**, sharing **one SQLite store** (`./selfdev.sqlite`) plus the
store's side files (`.broker.log`, `.broker.inbox/`); each seat is its **own OS process** with its **own worktree**, and
its conversation history lives in the **shared** store. So we are "many processes, one store", not "one process per
team" and not "one store per agent". The research prompt is commissioned and awaiting operator routing:
`docs/reviews/base-agent-product-topology-research-prompt.md` (asks 7 questions: process topology, store topology, the
base/team two-seam split, base-vs-extension policy in practice, per-agent memory/workspace ownership, documented
failure modes, and naming conventions with five real examples; it demands ≤40-word verbatim quotes + URL + fetch date,
because line ranges into an off-host agent's workspace are not portable — `docs/runbooks/research-request.md`).

**What the boundary actually looks like today (measured, not asserted).** The extension mechanism is real and already
used by the rig on itself: the config vocabulary registers `DURIG_EXTENSIONS` (`src/config.mjs:117`), the loader is
`loadExtensions` (`src/extensions.mjs:57`) taking an explicit comma-separated path list (`src/extensions.mjs:31`), and
the header states the trust boundary and the deliberate **absence of auto-discovery** — "which code runs in here must
stay an explicit operator decision". durian-pi registers five extensions on its own seats: `durig.router`
(`src/rig.mjs:617`, which carries `send_work`, `claim_work`, `complete_work`), `durig.seat-tools` (`src/seattools.mjs:238`,
which carries `prepare_workspace`, `seat_root`), `coding-tools` (`src/tui/durable/adapter.mjs:607`), plus
`src/seatguard.mjs` and the loader itself. So **the queue/role tool surface is already on the extension plane** — the
good news for this policy. The gap is size: **5 of 59** `src/*.mjs` files register a `defineExtension` (counted with
`grep -rln defineExtension src/ | wc -l` against `ls src/*.mjs | wc -l`), and the store, seat loop, broker and landing
path are built in. Also note the two-plane trap the loader documents: a **pi-durable** extension and a **pi-coding-agent**
extension are different things and cannot load into each other (`src/extensions.mjs`, header; ROADMAP 23) — any policy
gate must say *which* plane it means.

**Consequences the team must design in (decomposition is `lead`'s, not mine).** (a) The two minimum products need real
definitions, not a burn-down: `docs/MVP.md` is a **rig** burn-down from 2026-10-08 and carries the D103 pre-rename
banner, so it is the wrong home for a base-agent definition. (b) Testing must prove the policy rather than assert it:
a **base-boot-with-zero-extensions** gate (boots, converses, edits, survives a kill/restart with
`DURIG_EXTENSIONS` unset) and a **boundary gate** that refuses a new built-in customization the same way the docs gates
refuse a stale citation — the code analogue of ROADMAP 115/133, and cheap enough to run in `check`. (c) Every seat
turn already runs the *same* base with a different persona and extension list (`cli.mjs:463` loads per config), so the
"each member has their own instance" question is partly settled by the process model and only the **store** half is
open. (d) `docs/ROADMAP.md` must receive the resulting items as *registered, not scheduled*, and 128
("Extensibility surface") is now **policy-mandated** rather than a research suggestion.

**What only the operator can do.** Ratify the two product names (and the env/config prefix consequence); route the
research prompt to the off-host research agent. Neither is delegated by silence, and nothing here was renamed
unilaterally.

## D213 — Fast iteration is an architectural requirement: every piece must have a fast dev loop, and the slow part gets isolated behind a seam (operator ruling, 2026-11-05)

**Decision.** The operator ruled that we **architect for fast development iteration on the whole thing**, which
decomposes into three binding clauses:

1. **Break the system into pieces that each have a fast iteration loop of their own.** A piece whose loop is slow is a
   defect *in the architecture*, not a cost of doing business.
2. **Where a part restricts fast iteration, isolate it** — behind a seam, behind a boundary, out of the default loop —
   rather than letting its cost contaminate every change.
3. **The LLM is expected to be the slowest part, and it must be made iterable anyway** — explicitly allowing multiple
   techniques at once: prompt engineering, mocking, and smaller/faster models in test cases.

This is now a **review lens on every design row**: a proposal that lengthens the loop must say by how much and what seam
restores the fast path. Together with D212 (customization on the extension plane) it gives the rig two orthogonal
invariants — *where* code lives, and *how fast you can change it*.

**The measurement that reframes the operator's own hypothesis — and it is good news.** I ran the instruments instead of
guessing (Linux Fedora 45 `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64` node v24.22.1, same command as every number below):

- **The deterministic loop is already fast.** Full suite, parallel (`node scripts/test.mjs`, `DEFAULT_JOBS = min(8, cores)`
  at `scripts/test.mjs:41`): **`257/258 passed in 57.0s`**. Per-area: `broker` 63 tests / **25.4 s**, `rig` 63 / **24.0 s**,
  `tui` 46 / **12.4 s**, `toolchain` 16 / **11.1 s**, `worktree` 23 / **7.8 s**, `check` 12 / **6.3 s**, `readapi` 5 /
  **3.8 s**, `guard` 24 / **2.0 s**, `docs` 6 / **1.2 s**. The single worst test is `demo/cli.test.mjs` at **20.1 s** — one
  file is a third of the `rig` area's wall clock. **Correction to carry:** my own previous report recorded the suite as
  **1672 s**. That figure was a degraded (sequential / cold-deps, seat-root) run; the honest headline for the same 258 tests
  is **57 s parallel**, and the gap between 57 s and 1672 s is itself an iteration-cost finding — *how* you run the suite is a
  first-class variable, not a constant.
- **A mocked LLM already exists and is the fast path.** `@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/faux` (`fauxProvider`,
  `fauxText`, `fauxToolCall`, `fauxAssistantMessage`) is imported by **77 of 258** demos, and a **complete delegation loop**
  (pm → `send_work` → worker claims → completes → DONE notice back to pm) runs in **0.301 s** with no network and no keys
  (`node demo/offline.mjs`). So "make the LLM part iterable" is not a research question here — it is a *rule about which
  plane a behavior test is allowed to run on*. (Trap carried in that file's header: scripted faux responses **drain in
  global call order across conversations**, which is why ordering-sensitive tests are the ones that rot.)
- **Inside the LLM, the cost is a tail, not the typical turn.** `tools/latency-budget.mjs` (cost 3.1 s over 63,172
  generations, 47,353 tool tasks, 1,586 compactions): **model-call latency p50 52 ms, p95 9.0 s, p99 1.8 min, max 2.0 h**;
  **tool-call latency p50 59 ms, p95 4.7 s, p99 2.9 min, max 28.8 min**; **compaction p50 23.2 s, p95 4.2 min, max 8.3 h**
  (55.5 h of store lifetime). Generation buckets: 50.8% of runs finish in **0–5 s** and hold only **1.8%** of busy time,
  while **185 runs (0.29%) exceed 10 minutes and hold 517.5 h = 64.6% of generation busy time**. The top of that tail is not
  compute: ten generations of **~2,120 minutes** each (one per seat, `events=2–3`, `outcome=completed`) — a turn *staying
  open*, not a turn working. So the LLM part becomes iterable by **bounding turn lifetime and killing waste**, not by
  making typical calls faster.
- **The biggest latency in the rig is not the model at all.** Item latency decomposition: **WAIT (claimable, unclaimed) =
  72.4%**, WORK (claimed→done) = 13.0%, HELD = 5.9%; queue→done median 15.2 min, p95 9.3 h, max 295.3 h; and **308.7 h of
  store lifetime had 0 generations in flight** (channel down or idle). Provider waste: **14,377 generations, 22.5 h busy**,
  ending in refusals such as `402 You need positive balance` — the same class as this session's `401 Invalid API key`
  no-`--env-file` trap. Fast iteration for the *team* therefore means **fail before the call** and **shrink the WAIT**, not
  just faster tokens.

**What the policy therefore binds (the seams named in the ruling):**

- **The default loop must be hermetic.** One network-dependent test is enough to make the offline suite lie: today
  `demo/deepinfra-catalog.test.mjs` is **red without `DEEPINFRA_API_KEY`** in this shell (and in every fresh worktree) — a
  key-gated test inside the 57 s loop. Metered/vendor-catalog truth belongs in a separate, explicitly-invoked lane.
- **Behavior tests of seats run on faux by default**; a real model is an *opt-in* lane with a declared budget, and
  smaller/faster models are legitimate **in test cases** (the operator named this: test lanes may use a different model than
  production; the cross-family author/verifier invariant is a *production* rule and does not forbid a cheap test model).
- **Slow parts get a named boundary and a declared cost.** Every piece publishes its loop cost (seconds), and a gate fails
  when a piece's loop exceeds its budget — `check` currently has **no timing rule at all** (`grep -noE
  '"[a-z-]*(slow|latency|timeout|duration|budget)[a-z-]*"' src/checkup.mjs` → **zero hits**), and the only time bound in the
  config vocabulary is `DURIG_STREAM_TIMEOUT_MS` (`src/config.mjs:129`). There is no turn-lifetime cap.

## D216 — the operator answered eight things in eight lines, spent Round 2 of the topology research, ruled the idle-priority ordering, and rotated the credentials himself; B7 is the one item he sent back for explanation (2026-11-06T04:3xZ, delegate acting; Linux, Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five), kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node v24.22.1, git 2.56.0)

**Decision.** The operator's eight answers, in effect:

1. **Push — Approved.** `git push origin main` → `ef29516d..34324b62`; `git rev-list --count refs/remotes/origin/main..main` → `0`.
2. **Round 2 spend — the recommendation was approved.** Round 2 ran and landed at `docs/reviews/base-agent-product-topology-followup-research.md` (162 lines, 23,307 bytes). Its own budget disclosure: **5 of 5 tool iterations, 9 primary pages fetched, 6 result sets read, 1 failed fetch (`antigravity-cli-keep-going`)** — and it states plainly: "this round's stop was **budget-forced, not source-exhausted**" (source-pinned: that file, **Budget disclosure**). Recorded as part of the answer's cost, because it is why Q12 is closed only *as of 2026-11-06*.
3. **Backoff before capacity — Approved.** An ordering ruling, not a suggestion: **300 before any capacity change** (concurrency, verifier slot, per-seat caps). Its policy content is registered as ROADMAP **313**.
4. **B7 (per-agent database) — sent back: "Explain further and reevaluate after reading the followup research response."** Explanation, then re-evaluation, below.
5. **297 — Accepted:** measure three priced verify legs before touching the slot, "and consider what the current models are good at. If we are using bigger models for the verifier seat, maybe they are more efficient." The efficiency premise is now sourced rather than assumed — Q13 is the literature on a verifier being worth its per-token premium per defect found (source-pinned: `docs/reviews/base-agent-product-topology-followup-research.md` **Q13**).
6. **Hostname scrub — "Option 1 — Accepted."** Executed; the scope finding below matters more than the execution.
7. **Credential rotation — "Completed"** (by the operator). Verified from this side in the same command as the host signature: the free pre-flight still returns `"verdict": "ARMABLE"` for `openai/gpt-oss-120b` @ DeepInfra after the rotation, so rotating did not darken the family (`tools/verifier-arm-probe.mjs`, run 2026-11-06).
8. **Seat shell — "Accepted, with the `powershell` tool withheld on non-Windows hosts."** That chooses the durable fix over prompt-text mitigation, so it lands on ROADMAP **306** (per-seat extension/tool selection) and closes the open question on **302**. `src/seatguard.mjs:122` registers both `bash` and `powershell`; `:174-177` already admits that "a second copy of shell truth" is a smell — this ruling names that as the place to fix it.

**B7 explained — what "reject the per-agent database in writing" actually decides.** It is not a question about isolation. It is a question about **which layer isolation goes in**. Our store is one SQLite file with one single writer (D100). Per-seat databases would mean 12 stores, each with its own writer, its own cap ledger and its own model pins — and every defect measured this week multiplies by twelve under that shape: **299** (a dead pin darkens a seat) becomes twelve pin sets that can each go stale; **310** (a cap ledger that silently resets) becomes twelve ledgers that can each reset; **303** (one dark read path) becomes twelve. And the isolation that would be bought is isolation we already have at the layer shipped systems actually use: **one worktree and one scratch root per seat** (`src/seatroot.mjs`, `src/worktree.mjs`) — file-level separation, one event log above it.

**Re-evaluated after Round 2 — the ruling strengthens, and Round 2 sharpens what we keep.** Q12 was the falsifier hunt and it came back empty in a more useful way than a counterexample: for every vendor examined, the per-agent unit is a **machine or a workspace**, never a database inside a team — Cursor runs each background agent in its **own VM with snapshot/resume**, Jules in **per-task VMs** (source-pinned: `docs/reviews/base-agent-product-topology-followup-research.md`, **Q12** Cursor and Jules rows). So the shipped pattern is **one durable store per team, one isolated filesystem per agent** — which is exactly the topology already running here. The written rejection should therefore be two clauses, not one: **(a)** reject per-seat *databases*; **(b)** affirm per-seat *workspaces/worktrees* as the shipped analogue we keep. The hosted split Q12 also names — one disposable VM per *unattended* task — is a fact about unattended modes, not an argument for per-seat stores in an interactive team.

**Where that sits:** the **written** rejection is the operator's act — B7 asks for a `docs/DECISIONS.md` row with a reason and a date, and an architecture ruling signed by a delegate is not a ruling. The wording above is ready for him to adopt or amend; I did not write it for him.

**The scrub executed, and the scope finding that came out of it.** Option 1 was implemented literally — replace the transient hostname with `label-withheld-per-D205` **only on lines already carrying a real host signature (`fc44`/`fc45`)**, keeping distro, kernel, node and git. Measured result: **14 files touched, 33 occurrences replaced** (`git diff --stat`: 33 insertions, 33 deletions; script `.spike/delegate-20261106/scrub-hostname.mjs`). Two things learned doing it: **(a)** the first attempt *deleted* the token and left dangling punctuation — empty backticks, `box )` — which reads as corpus corruption; a placeholder that states why is the right shape, and `git diff | grep -c '``'` → `0` is the check that v2 passes. **(b)** the accepted scope **does not reach the damage it was meant to reach**: of the hostname occurrences still in tracked docs, **49 are the *other* box's label — the one ending in `-Win10` that D205 names as the false-attribution case — and not one of those 49 lines carries an `fc44`/`fc45` signature**, so option 1 leaves every one of them in place. The mislabel is still in the record: `docs/DECISIONS.md:6439`, `:6470`, `:6555`, `:7028` assert a Linux host under a Windows-suffixed name. I did not exceed the granted scope. The extension to put to him (**1b**): replace that label on lines that assert **Linux**, leaving genuine Windows-era records alone. The forward-facing half — nothing new may sign work with a hostname — is registered as ROADMAP **320**, with B9's caveat carried on the row: a gate can check host *shape*, because the project cannot know which names are transient (`static unset`, `/etc/hostname` empty).

**Round 2's backlog is registered as ROADMAP 313–319** — registration is the delegate's act per **298**; acceptance and sequencing are `lead`'s. Two of its proposals need correcting against what our own corpus already holds, and both corrections make the row cheaper: recorded in `docs/reviews/base-agent-product-topology-followup-research.md` **## Delegate diff**.

- **R2-5 (Goose recipes) under-evidences the one vendor we have pinned.** It cites `documentation/docs/recipes/...`, while `docs/COMPETITORS.md:380` pins `goose` at `775b3958` with the **full Rust source** read and `:396-397` already cites `crates/goose/src/recipe/local_recipes.rs:155,194`. The §3 source-audit protocol in the prompt was not applied where we already hold the artifact. The claim is probably right; the evidence should be the pin.

## D224 — the operator rules that pi-ecosystem alignment is a product requirement and that there are **no Windows seats for a long time**; the delegate's other recommendations are accepted, and this decision also corrects three pointers the delegate shipped wrong (2026-11-06T21:5xZ, delegate acting; host signature measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v && git --version` → Linux, `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five), node v24.22.1, git 2.56.0)

Nothing in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` or `~/.pi/agent/models.json` reaches a seat. Registered as **ROADMAP 332** with four named seams (S1 settings, S2 model registry, S3 credentials, S4 visibility + pin currency) and **331 as slice 1 of S1**, because 331 is the one seam half already measured end-to-end with a free probe. This is a **D212 base seam**, not a customization: a seat's config *input* is not an extension, and per D212 the fact that it cannot be expressed as an extension is evidence the base is missing the seam.

**Ruling 2 — the drift between the two planes is already measurable, and it is not cosmetic.** Same model, two planes: the seat plane sets `DURIG_LOCAL_CONTEXT = 200000` (`durig.config.json:5`) while pi's registry says `strata/qwen3.8-flash-next-iq3_s contextWindow 204800, maxTokens 32768` and `strata-server/… 131072 / 24576` — **three context windows for one model name**, and that integer feeds the compaction threshold (331), the `compact` report's `declaredContextWindow` (`cli.mjs:1595`) and the spend math (141, 326). Thinking level is duplicated the same way (`defaultThinkingLevel: "medium"` in pi vs `"thinkingLevel": "high"` in `rig.selfdev.json`). The verifier family exists on **one** plane only — pi's `models.json` has no DeepInfra/`verifier` provider — so "just read pi's registry" would delete the cross-family author/verifier invariant `src/providers/local.mjs:9-34` exists to protect (D48/D119). And seat turns are invisible to pi's surfaces: `~/.pi/agent/sessions` holds 6 entries, 0 naming a seat worktree.

**Ruling 3 — no Windows seats for a long time. What that parks, and what it pointedly does not.** Parked: the Windows-side *observation* work — **#5278** (`qa`, "verify 311(ii) from a Windows host") stays `held` and is **no longer on the critical path**, and the Windows worktree-audit ask (**#5285**) is parked. ## D225 — the credential/secret question is researched and the evidence is landed; **333 stays open because the fork is the operator's**, and the sweep finds that a separate secrets service is *not* automatically a boundary on this rig (2026-11-07T02:2xZ, delegate acting; host signature measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v && git --version` → Linux, `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five), node v24.22.1, git 2.56.0)

**What the operator asked, in the operator's words.** Research *before deciding* how other agent frameworks and agent teams manage credentials/secrets **between members** — "is the credential pass to all members, to specific members or the team leader? does the credential service hold the credential and only the service use them or what else do they do?" — with the operator's own hypothesis that "the best architecture would be a separate process or service that holds secrets", and a mid-session addition: **include oh-my-pi** (`github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi`) in the research.

**Method, so the coverage is auditable.** Read the upstream-read surface (runbook `competitor-review.md`), never a secondary report: **ten clones** read at their measured pins (`vendor/pi-main @ 2ec55d80` — note: **not** under `vendor/eval/`; `vendor/eval/{oh-my-pi 6f3fbc94, openhands 6354932e, codex d373d649, goose 775b3958, claude-code-docs 58d6da1e, cline 51f63e4f, crewai f3d0099d, pi-subagents 31208242, prime-agent 815e64b5}`; every HEAD re-measured with `git -C … rev-parse --short=8 HEAD` **in the same turn as this sentence**), plus two vendor docs (`spire` concepts, `litellm-models` proxy) **labelled `advertised-elsewhere`** and not credited as clone evidence. `node tools/vendor-pins.mjs --check` → **PIN CHECK PASS, 27 clones** (it also audits reviews: a review naming a present clone cites its HEAD and has a `docs/COMPETITORS.md` entry). Evidence: `docs/reviews/credentials-in-agent-teams-competitor-sweep-2026-11-07.md` (mechanisms M1–M12, coverage matrix, per-mechanism adopt/adapt/reject), decision rows in `docs/COMPETITORS.md`, options in `docs/reviews/credential-architecture-options-2026-11-07.md`, follow-up prompt in `docs/reviews/credentials-secret-brokerage-followup-research-prompt.md`.

**Ruling 1 — the fork (ROADMAP 333) is NOT taken, and the research strengthens the objection to option (b) with a mechanism, not a vibe.** pi's resolver states the precedence (`vendor/pi-main/packages/ai/src/auth/resolve.ts:28-35`): *"A stored credential owns the provider: ambient/env is consulted only when nothing is stored. No silent env fallback after a failed refresh."* So if durian-pi read pi's store, `DURIG_VERIFIER_API_KEY` would be **ignored, not overridden** — a seat would authenticate as whatever the human logged in as, `selfdev.sqlite.spend.jsonl`'s `authKeyEnv` attribution would go false, and a rotation would stay invisible (326). The role→family guarantee (D48/D119) and the loopback-only `local` rule (325) both depend on durian-pi choosing the credential per **role**, which a shared store cannot express.

**Ruling 2 — the measured hole is not the fork; it is reachability, and it exists today.** All 12 seats are conversations inside one broker process (`cli.mjs:474`, `cli.mjs:479`) and their shells are its children, same uid. `src/confine.mjs` strips credential-named env from the child env it builds (measured: 0 key-shaped names cross; canary `demo/confine.test.mjs` PASS 0.37 s), **but** a seat-shaped shell printed **92 env names from `/proc/<pid>/environ`, including `DURIG_VERIFIER_API_KEY` and `DURIG_LOCAL_API_KEY`**, and `refusalFor("cat /proc/$PPID/environ")` returned **no refusal** (probe: `.spike/delegate-20261107/envprobe/procfs-canary.mjs`, ~6 s, canary values, names only). Our value classifier would likely not report the leak either: `looksLikeSecret` (`src/config.mjs:73-82`) needs a known prefix **or** ≥40 chars **and** a digit (measured: 32-char alnum → `false`). **Therefore the current control is "a seat doesn't think to ask", which is not a control** — and it is fixable for $0 without waiting for the fork (rows **336**, **337**).

**Ruling 3 — the operator's instinct is right in shape and wrong in one specific default: a separate service that hands out *values* moves the secret, it does not hide it.** Three shipped strengths exist, and only the last two are boundaries here: **openhands** keeps secrets behind a service addressed by **name** with an ask-the-human tool, but "exposed to this conversation as an environment variable named after the secret" — the value still lands in the consumer's env; **codex** keeps the value in the **proxy** and gives the child a dummy/marker (`credential_broker.rs:44-51`, `CredentialMaskingFailureMode{Warn,Deny,Error}`), but only for HTTP through its egress proxy; **oh-my-pi** (the closest comparator, inside our own substrate's ecosystem) runs a separate `auth-broker` holding the vault, whose refresh token *"never leaves the broker host"* (`remote-store.ts:1290-1318`, enforced as **two types**: `wire-schemas.ts:55-63` narrows a real credential's `refresh` to not equal `REMOTE_REFRESH_SENTINEL`), and an `auth-gateway` through which members make provider requests *"without ever receiving provider credentials"*, with per-client `models`/`accounts` grants answered `404`/`400` **before any credential lookup**, usage/quota at the holder, and a `stdio` variant for *"one trusted parent process: no listener, no token"* — which is exactly the shape this rig has (one broker process, seats as children). **A loopback bearer token is reachable by the same `/proc` probe that reached the key**, so a network secrets service on a single-uid host buys governance, not reachability (row **340** is the governance pilot; **342** is the boundary spike).

**Ruling 4 — what the delegate did and did not do.** Registered rows **334–342** (the `CredentialStore` seam, the ask-the-operator path, the classifier floor, the `/proc` path + presence policy, command-resolved credentials + an `auth check` probe, the keychain/stdin/argv rule, the per-consumer budget pilot, credential-lookup ordering, and the request-level gateway spike). **The delegate did not rule 333, did not touch any credential value, did not start a service, and did not spend model money** (all canaries are local; the only provider calls were 3 preflight probes, measured at **$0.00123** when they ran — and
**corrected at clock-out**: that cost does **not** appear in `selfdev.sqlite.spend.jsonl`, whose last row is
`2026-11-06T18:26:30.110Z` (`856` rows, `usd 0.34959`), so a delegate-run preflight probe spends money the family tripwire
cannot see — a fresh specimen for **310** ("there are two spend ledgers, neither is tracked"), and the reason the delegate
must quote the tripwire's number, not its own arithmetic.) The recommendation, with pros/cons and the operator-only list, is in `docs/reviews/credential-architecture-options-2026-11-07.md`: **answer 333 as (a) env-only + the visibility tax, fund 336/337/341 now (free), fund 334/338 as 332-S3, then pilot 342; do not adopt a network secrets service before 342 is measured.**

**Ruling 5 — a scope addition mid-session is handled by extending the sweep, not restarting it.** The operator named
oh-my-pi after the first draft; the sweep was extended (its `docs/auth-broker-gateway.md` and `docs/secrets.md` read in
full, and `packages/ai/src/auth-broker/{remote-store,wire-schemas,snapshot-cache}.ts` opened) and it **changed the

**CORRECTION (2026-11-07T04:3xZ, same session, before the operator ruled 333) — Ruling 1 over-stated the objection to (b).**
Re-reading the resolver in full: `resolve.ts:67-84` prefers a stored credential *harness-side*, but every api-key path ends
in `resolveApiKey` (`resolve.ts:193-205`), which **always** invokes the provider's own

`resolve.ts:29-30` ("no silent env fallback") constrains the *harness's* fallback, not our resolver. This materially lowers
the cost of (b) — and the operator chose (b), as a swappable interface, in the same session (**D227**). The reachability
finding in Ruling 2 (`/proc/<pid>/environ`, row 337) is **unaffected**: it is about who can read a value already resident,

## D227 — the operator **rules 333 = (b), as a user-swappable interface with a recommended implementation and a bare-bones env/file default**, **approves 338 ("Go ahead with it")** and **approves landing 331**; rotation rides the store, not a restart (2026-11-07T04:3xZ, delegate recording; host signature measured with `uname -s && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v && git --version` → **Linux**, Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five), node v24.22.1, git 2.56.0)

**The ruling, in the operator's words.** *"I prefer (b), but only because we can treat it as an interface that can be swapped by the user. There are many credential store implementations, such as the Hashicorp Vault, Microsoft has one, KDE has one, etc. We should provide a recommended implementation, but leave a bare-bones implementation that pulled it from an env var or local file like Pi does."* On rotation: *"We can implement rotations more easily if we have a credential store interface and implementation. But we can try your recommendation. Go ahead with it."* And: *"Land 331, approved."*

**What this decides, precisely.** (1) **333 is closed as a fork and opened as a build**: the rig ships the pi-shaped `CredentialStore` **interface** plus **one bare-bones default** (env var / local file, pi-shaped) plus **one recommended implementation**, and third-party backends (HashiCorp Vault, Windows Credential Manager, KDE KWallet, macOS Keychain) are user-swappable. (2) **338 (`auth check`) is scheduled work** — the masked keycheck in `.spike/delegate-20261106c/` gets promoted under carrier `#5277`. (3) **331 is approved to land** (the compaction-override nesting fix), and it stays the first thing run because it gates any context-band work in the new milestone. (4) **Rotation becomes a store operation** — `modify(providerId, fn)` under the store's per-provider lock (`types.ts:80-91`) replaces "restart the broker and hope". The **cadence** question stays the operator's.

**Why the operator's reading is technically right, measured in this tree (this turn, not from memory).** The seam already exists and we are already standing in it: `CreateModelsOptions.credentials?: CredentialStore` (`vendor/pi-main/packages/ai/src/models.ts:375`) is applied as `this.credentials = options?.credentials ?? new InMemoryCredentialStore()` (`models.ts:407`, class at `auth/credential-store.ts:9`), and **`cli.mjs:391` is the only live `createModels(` call site** (`cli.mjs:322` is the faux branch, deliberately unauthenticated). So durian-pi is not "declining a store" in the strong sense — it is running pi's **empty in-memory default** and overriding the ambient plane with `authContext` (`cli.mjs:391-397`). Two more facts that de-risk the switch: **all three providers already implement pi's auth shape** (`cli.mjs:353-358`; `src/providers/local.mjs:306-316` returns `{auth:{apiKey:key}, source:keyEnv}` from env and the loopback placeholder with `source:"none"` otherwise), so **one injected store covers every seat**; and a stored credential does **not** silence our resolver — `resolve.ts:67-84` prefers it harness-side, but `resolveApiKey` (`resolve.ts:193-205`) always calls our `apiKey.resolve({ctx, credential, signal})`. See the **CORRECTION appended to D225**: my earlier "stored-wins would break the family guarantee" was too strong, and the correction does **not** touch D225 Ruling 2's `/proc` reachability finding, which stands on its own evidence.

**Rows updated, not invented:** 333 now carries the ruling verbatim and stays open only for *which implementation is the recommended one*; **334** was corrected (its registered interface signature `{id, name, sourceHint, list, get, nonInteractive, modify}` at `types.ts:41-100` is **wrong** — the interface is `read`/`list`/`modify`/`delete` at `types.ts:65-97`, a D159-class citation defect in a row the delegate itself registered last session) and now names the swap point (`models.ts:375`/`:407` at `cli.mjs:391`) and the resolver-still-runs fact; **338** is marked approved with the observation that `list()` (`types.ts:72-77`) answers credential **presence** for free, so the probe's job narrows to *usability*; **339** is reframed (an OS keychain is a candidate *backend*, not a separate practice); **326** now points at `modify()` for rotation and names the cadence question as the operator's.

**What the delegate did NOT do.** Chose the recommended backend (the operator's call — options below); claim, complete or route a queue row; write store code (that is a seat's work — the delegate spooled the ruling to `lead` via `node intent.mjs lead --body-file …` per `docs/SELFDEV.md:80`, never inline); start the broker; touch a credential value; spend model money.

### The four decisions still needed, with options and the delegate's recommendation

**A. Which implementation is the rig's *recommended* one (333's only open half).**
**(i) the bare-bones file default, promoted to recommended** — pro: no new moving part, no daemon, works under the native-host rule (D131) and headless; con: file-protected-only, and 337 already proved same-uid reachability is our weak edge. **(ii) an OS credential service backend** (KWallet here; Windows Credential Manager / macOS Keychain elsewhere) — pro: the ecosystem answer, per-user ACLs, matches 339's keychain-first rule, and it is a *backend* so it costs nothing in the base; con: it is a session-bound daemon (headless/SSH rigs frequently have none), and its security domain is the login session, not the rig. **(iii) HashiCorp Vault backend** — pro: rotation, TTLs, leases and per-consumer budgets land in one place (it is F1 with a vendor), best fit for 324/340; con: it is exactly the network listener + capacity + credential to-the-credential-store decision the operator declined for F1 on 2026-11-07. **Recommendation: recommend (i) now — a 0600 file at a rig-owned path with explicit source attribution — and ship (ii) as the first optional backend, with (iii) deferred until 342's measurement says whether the rig wants request-level brokerage (which makes a remote store redundant for the model path).** Any backend choice other than (i) needs an operator grant of a new moving part; the delegate will not install one.
**B. What the store is keyed by.** pi keys by `Provider.id`, one credential per provider (`types.ts:52-53`). Our provider ids are **already role-shaped** — `LOCAL_PROVIDER_ID = "local"`, `VERIFIER_PROVIDER_ID = "verifier` (`src/providers/local.mjs:33-34`) and the metered provider id at `cli.mjs:350` — so role scoping survives pi's keying **as long as that 1:1 holds**. Options: **(i) keep provider-id keying and enforce role↔provider-id 1:1 as a `check` finding**; **(ii) ask pi upstream for a scoped key (`providerId + scope`)** — the pi-alignment-first ruling (D224) favours raising it, but it is an upstream dependency we'd then wait on; **(iii) invent a rig-side composite id** (`verifier#lead`) — pro: per-seat grants without touching pi, and it is 342's grant surface; con: it fakes identity with strings and will drift. **Recommendation: (i) now with a `check` assertion, (iii) only inside the 342 spike where the grant is the point, and (ii) as a question filed upstream, not a dependency.** A `check` finding is the cheap guarantee (307's precedent).
**C. Precedence when a store entry and a `DURIG_*` env value both exist.** Options: **(i) pi's default** (stored wins, ambient consulted only when nothing is stored); **(ii) env wins** (an explicit launch-time value means "use this now", which is how rotation-by-restart works today); **(iii) fail loud** — refuse the provider and name both sources; **(iv) explicit-source-wins**: the config names the source per family (`DURIG_VERIFIER_CRED_SOURCE=env|store:<name>`) and a second, unrequested source is a refusal. **Recommendation: (iv), because 341's rule is "no silent fallback", and because the ledger's `authKeyEnv` column (`src/providers/local.mjs:294`, `authKeyEnv` carried so the row can say which variable paid) only means something if the source is chosen deliberately.** (i) is defensible for pi-ecosystem sameness but would silently out-rank an operator's launch-time rotation, which is the exact failure **326** records.
**D. Does a seat ever hold the value?** This is 342's design fork and it is now the *only* credential question with a money/capacity dimension. Options: **(i) status quo** — the broker resolves at request time and the seat never holds a key for the model path (true today: `auth.apiKey.resolve` runs broker-side at `cli.mjs:353-358`, and pi's own OAuth design comment warns against handing a client a live refresh token, `auth/types.ts:118-127`); **(ii) hand seats a per-seat scoped credential** from the store — pro: works for consumers the broker cannot proxy (git, package registries, the seat's own shell); con: it puts a real value into a same-uid child, which 337 measured as readable through `/proc`; **(iii) hand seats a request-level grant** (the oh-my-pi `stdio` gateway shape, and prime-agent's `get_api_key` resolver, M12) — pro: the value never lands in the child; con: only covers consumers that ask rather than connect. **Recommendation: keep (i) for the model path, pilot (iii) for everything else, and treat (ii) as a fall-back that requires closing 337 first.** If the operator wants option (ii) anyway, that is a capacity/policy grant, not a technical one.

config names 'qwen3.8-flash-next-iq3_s'`.

## D240 — the operator re-orders the milestone: **avoid compaction; continuation notes are the mechanism, and they live on the extension plane** (2026-11-09T03:2xZ, delegate recording; host measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v && git --version` → **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**, `git version 2.56.0`)

**The ruling, as given.** "The priority is to avoid context compaction. If a task cannot be completed in a single
context window, ensure the team member is properly maintaining notes to ensure they can continue working on the task
from a fresh context, in case the team harness forces them to work in a new context." The operator did not know where
the notes should live or whether that should be configurable per installation, and ruled the mechanism must be **an
extension**, "as is proper in the Pi ecosystem" (D212: a customization that cannot be an extension means the base is
missing a seam — grow the seam, not the feature).

**What the delegate adopted, and the measurement behind each choice.**

1. **Source of truth is a store document**, `defineDoc({kind: "durig.notes", scope: "conversation", history: "rewindable", fork: "asOf"})` — the shape
   ROADMAP **177** already ruled for typed state, and the shape the pi-durable `PlanDoc` example uses. *Why not a file
   in the seat's worktree:* `.durig/` is gitignored (`.gitignore:16`), seats work in per-item worktrees (D49), and the
   rig has a recorded incident where worktree and scratch state were swept
   (`docs/incidents/2026-10-26-worktree-and-scratch-sweep.md`). A note that dies with the worktree is not a continuity
   mechanism, and a gate cannot read it.
2. **A mirror file, configurable per installation:** `DURIG_NOTES_DIR/item-<id>.md`, default `<rig root>/.durig/notes/`,
   resolved through `src/config.mjs` like every other setting and printed by `check` so the effective path is never
   guessed. This answers the operator's "configurable per installation" question with one env var, not a new config
   surface.
3. **Compaction stays as a fallback, but the summariser model call is removed.** `beforeCompact`
   (`pi-durable dist/harness/compaction.js:82-88`) lets an extension return `{summary}` and `place()` commits it at
   `:374` — the summariser request is never constructed. That deletes the fragile part: **218** "Summarization hit
   the token limit; the summary is incomplete" records, **209** refusals by `DURIG_SPEND_CAP_RUN_USD` before any
   request was sent, and 1 provider 429, out of **2,333** attempts (430 failed). It does **not** `{decline: true}`:
   ROADMAP **176** forbids a competing summariser, and the hook writing the summary *is* pi-durable's own mechanism.
4. **The note is not put in the prompt.** ROADMAP **175** is the gate — pi-durable rebuilds the system prompt from
   sections before every request and provider caching is prefix-exact, so a `render` that changes per request may be a
   full-prefix cache miss every request. Static pointer section only; the mutable body arrives at boundaries: wake
   (`src/driver.mjs:54, 242`), compaction (`beforeCompact`), and reset (`src/reset.mjs:70`, `harness.reset(handoff)`
   at `dist/harness/harness.js:45-48`). The reset path matters because a compaction summary is *always* fenced
   (`compaction.js:12-13, :374`), so a structured seed can only come from a reset.
5. **The 331 nesting fix is still required** — as the fallback's plumbing, not as the milestone. `src/config.mjs:513`
   emits `out.modelOverrides` as a sibling of `compaction`, which `dist/harness/compaction.js:196` never reads, and
   `demo/config.test.mjs:333-341` asserts the sibling shape, so the test currently pins the bug (pitfall 161).

**Why this ordering, and not "make compaction better."** Compaction cannot be the answer to task completion because
the wall is not the window. Measured this session: the auditor's live context is **106 %** of its declared 24,576-token
window; **9 of 12 seats** are `AT RISK` on turn shape — a strict alternating template refuses the next user turn before
any token limit is reached; and a seat's current window carries **1–11 queue items** (impl references 108 distinct
`item-\d+` in its last 200 entries), so the summariser is being asked to compress a hundred unrelated tasks. A perfect
summary of a window holding a hundred tasks still does not let one task finish. The note is the unit of continuity;
the window is just where it is carried.

**Deliberately left to the operator.** Whether the verifier/auditor moves to the local family (it is the seat at the
wall — every one of the 209 run-cap refusals belongs to conversation 4936) or whether `DURIG_VERIFIER_MAX_TOKENS` /
verifier context is raised: capacity is a grant, not a delegate action. Whether notes are per-project or per-rig is
already answered by D130/R1 (per project; this rig is one project today).

**Recorded, not done.** No code was written by this delegate. The design is
`docs/reviews/architecture-context-continuity-2026-11-09.md`; the intent is spooled to `pm` as
`delegate-20261109-continuity` (broker `pid 114848`, first pass `INTENT delivered=5 dead=0 dup=0`).

## D241 — 2026-11-09T04:4xZ: landing becomes a **role**, not an errand — a release seat owns the readiness plan, the quiesce-then-merge pass stays outside the broker (operator question, delegate answer; host measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v && git --version` → **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**, `git version 2.56.0`)

**The decision.** The operator asked whether the team should have a release manager / ops seat responsible for
merging all completed branches, instead of the delegate landing them by hand. The delegate agrees, and records the
shape the role can actually take, because the rig already contains the constraint that decides it.

**Why the naive version cannot work.** `docs/runbooks/land.md:427-431`, read in-tree: "**A landing pass CANNOT be
driven by a broker-hosted seat.** Quiescing requires stopping the broker, and stopping the broker ENDS the run of any
seat hosted by it — so such a seat cannot stop the broker and then land and report. (2026-10-17: the exclusive
landing window closed QUIET BUT EMPTY for exactly this reason.)" The same runbook states plainly that `land` is the
delegate's/operator's action, not the team's. So "the ops seat merges everything" is not implementable today; a seat
that stops the broker stops itself.

**What the role CAN own (measured need, 04:4xZ).** `git branch --list` → 151 item branches; **62 ahead of `main**;
**83 commits** unlanded; `git merge-tree --write-tree main <branch>` → **43 merge clean, 19 conflict**. This recurs
after every pass: `docs/DECISIONS.md:7404` requires re-establishing the seat-root invariant after every landing pass,
and ROADMAP 311 records 21 worktrees the rig classified as `reapable` and nothing consumed — the delegate removed them
by hand. ROADMAP 310 shows the land helper refuses the whole train on a dirty tree, and the dirt was the rig's own
`selfdev.sqlite.spend.jsonl`. That is a continuous job with a name, not an occasional favour.

**The split, spooled to `pm` as `delegate-20261109-release-role`:**
- **Part A, seat-ownable, no model spend:** keep the landing list current against the three gates in
  `docs/BRANCH-AND-WORKTREE-LIFECYCLE.md` §5 (verified in queue; tip matches the landing list vs `git rev-parse`;
  clean against the **current** `main` by `git merge-tree`); order the train and name every stacked entry's base
  (`land.md:400-410`); report the conflict set with a named owner per conflict; own worktree/branch hygiene.
  Acceptance: one command prints an ordered, executable plan; after a pass `git rev-list --count main..<branch>` is 0

- **Part B, not seat-ownable:** the quiesce-then-merge act. If the team wants it inside the rig, it is a **base seam**

**Deliberately left to the operator.** Creating a new seat is a capacity grant: 12 seats today, `DURIG_MAX_CONCURRENT_SEATS = 4` (D238), and 9 of 12 seats are already `AT RISK` on turn shape — adding a seat is not free. The operator decides whether the role is a new seat, a redefinition of `lead` (which already writes landing entries) or `devtools` (which owns rebase-then-land per DISPOSITIONS:200), or a delegate-run cadence with the seat only preparing the plan.

**Recorded, not done.** No branch was merged by this session. `main` = `429f2b5a` (docs + gate only).

## D242 — One ledger reader, one host-qualified verdict, no unscoped prune: the shape `pruneWorktrees` and the broker sweep must converge on (architect, item #4846, 2026-11-06)

**Status.** Proposed. It is the **design-of-record that opens the gate on #4850 / ROADMAP 232** (241's closure signal:
the note must exist before 232 is claimed), and it is *not* 232 — no code changed here. Full note with the measured
probe output: `docs/reviews/worktree-seat-state-resolution-2026-11-06.md`.

**Context.** Four things resolve the same question — "is this registered working tree known to this host, and is it
ours?" — and only the blind one has a destructive verb: `pruneWorktrees` (`src/worktree.mjs:649-658`, called from
`src/broker.mjs:1167`, `src/worktree.mjs:667`, `src/worktree.mjs:1326`), `classifyWorktrees`'s `norm`
(`src/broker.mjs:989`), `resolveSeatRoot`/`sameRoot` (`src/seatroot.mjs:28-38`), and a *third* inline normalizer 263 did
not count (`src/broker.mjs:1069`). The seam defect is exact: the sweep reads the ledger **non-strict**
(`src/broker.mjs:1065`, and `cleanVerifyScratch` at `:1091` — an act-caller), so a failed read yields `[]`
(`src/worktree.mjs:1414`) and the sweep reaps nothing — **and then prunes unconditionally anyway**
(`src/broker.mjs:1167`, its own comment: *"whether or not it removed anything this pass"*). **The destructive act is not
gated by the same predicate as the read.** That is the mechanism of the 36 → 1 ledger collapse
(`docs/incidents/2026-10-28-cross-os-ledger-pruned-and-untracked-loss.md`) and of a demo suite pruning a checkout it was
never meant to touch.

**Options considered.** (A) *git-native quarantine only* — the workspace-move runbook locks every foreign-shaped
registration so any prune skips it: cheapest, fully reversible, but protects only what was locked first. (B) *scope the
plane* — one reader, computed verdicts, act per name, quarantine the rest, report N: narrower blast radius, but more code
in the most safety-loaded path, and it depends on 263's resolver. (C) *never prune* — reject as primary (ghost
registrations are real; 25 were cleared on 2026-10-19 per `src/broker.mjs:1164-1166`), retain only as the shape of a
named operator verb.

**Decision: B, with A shipped as the interim act.** Rules: **D-a** one ledger reader, extended to carry the `prunable
<reason>` line git already emits, and every act-caller passes `{strict:true}`; **D-b** a host-qualified verdict per row
(`this-host-present` / `this-host-missing` / `foreign` / `unknown`) computed by 263's resolver, and only
`this-host-missing` may be cleared; **D-c** foreign/unknown rows are **quarantined (locked) and recorded**, never
cleared — measured that a lock survives `prune` and is reversible by `unlock`; **D-d** no bare `git worktree prune` from
any decision path (delete the unconditional calls; any surviving prune is a named verb with an allow-list *and* git's
`--expire` grace); **D-e** N is never silent (diagnostic + attention row + `--status`, beside the existing count in
`tools/instrument-provenance.mjs:130`); **D-f** `unknown` beats `keep` beats `act` — if the resolver cannot classify a
stored seat root, the sweep skips itself and reports rather than running with a guard that cannot fire (266).

**Consequences.** The transferable part of the Codex research (241) is *reachability, not verb-matching*
(`core-plugins/src/git_policy.rs:7-85`, via `docs/reviews/codex-enforcement-design-2026-10-28.md` §3): a runtime guard on
the broker's own call is unenforceable because the broker calls itself (`docs/ROADMAP.md` 241 Do-not), so the design
removes the plane instead of intercepting it. A wrong prune turns out to be **less** catastrophic for tracked work than
the incident reads — registrations go, refs survive (measured: `git for-each-ref` still listed every branch after their
registrations were pruned) — so the loss to protect is the **ledger as evidence** (209-214, 212's input) and untracked
work, which need different controls. Two costs named, not hidden: (1) B adds code to the sweeper, and quarantine can
strand a reapable row, so the quarantine must be recorded with an owner and a `reviewBy` (F5/F6); (2) the lock is **not**
a general barrier — `removeClaimedWorktree` unlocks by design (`src/worktree.mjs:1207-1229`), so the *record* of the
verdict is the authority for our own verbs (F11). And the instrument that appears to cover this is not honest: `node
tools/rig-portability-audit.mjs --self-test` measured `SELF-TEST PASS … for a foreign-OS root: not-terminal` (exit 0) —
it asserts the classifier's current behaviour, so it certifies the hole; it must assert the protective property and go
red until 263/266 land.


## D243 — a roadmap row is bounded by its acceptance check, not by its design note (2026-11-06; architect acting, on lead's ruling in queue #5208)

**Status.** Accepted and in force for every new row and every proposed fold. Docs-only; no code touched.

**Context.** I deferred #5048 to settle whether a design intent is one roadmap row or two. The question recurs every session and each recurrence costs a lead round-trip; meanwhile the answer that is *not* taken is cheap and destructive — rows get merged because the roadmap reads shorter. Detail and worked examples: `docs/reviews/architecture-row-shape-fold-rule-2026-11-06.md`.

**Decision.** The unit of a roadmap row is **one independently-red acceptance check**, not one design note and not one concern-as-prose.
- FOLD only when all three hold: one acceptance command goes red for either half; they cannot land independently (same branch, same commit); split, one half would be true but unactionable.
- STAND BESIDE when any one holds: each half has its own command that can go red independently; different seats or different times can claim them; one half is naming/observability and the other is behavior.
- Folding to shorten `docs/ROADMAP.md` is refused.
- Falsifiable probe (measured, exit 0, main @ `46c28b73`): count each row's own `*Acceptance:*` clause — `awk '/^[0-9]+\. /{if(n!="")printf "row %s own-Acceptance=%d\n", n, c; n=$1; c=0} /\*Acceptance:\*/{c++} END{if(n!="")printf "row %s own-Acceptance=%d\n", n, c}' docs/ROADMAP.md` — ROADMAP 92/93/94/95 each carry exactly 1, naming four different assertions, so none may be folded into another. A row with 0 is a fold candidate or an untestable row; either way it is the row to fix.
- Applied: #2402 folds into **92** (`docs/ROADMAP.md:1806-1821`) and #2403 into **94** (`docs/ROADMAP.md:1833-1840`), because both halves already live on the durable surface — D107 at `docs/DECISIONS.md:2880`, its cap-at-2-then-re-anchor parameter with the 94 pointer at `docs/DECISIONS.md:2934`, the ordering at `docs/DECISIONS.md:2936`. #2619 stands beside, and the capacity fold is not a candidate for it: its citation of a cancelled item is provenance, not a gate (`docs/reviews/architecture-queue-lifecycle-redesign-review.md:395-397`). #94 stands beside the send-time bounding work, and the vocabulary row #5206 stands beside its carrier #4973.

**Options considered.** (a) *Group rows by concern* — fewer rows, one design note per theme; rejected because a green run then cannot say which half regressed, and the half that regressed is exactly the one that was merged in. (b) *One row per sentence* — maximum signal; rejected because it splits a single acceptance check across rows that must land in the same commit, so a seat can close one half and call the pair done. (c) *Keep asking lead per case* — rejected as the status quo ante: it spends a ruling per session and remembers nothing. (d) *Chosen*: the acceptance check bounds the row; the design note may span many rows and cross-links them instead of merging them.

**Consequences.** Every row must keep its own `*Acceptance:*` and `*Owner:*` line, or the probe flags it; cross-references ("vocabulary row names its carrier row") become the way pairs are shown, so the roadmap grows in cross-links rather than in merged rows — accepted, since length is not the property being protected. The one part the probe cannot decide, two clauses naming the same assertion in different words, stays a human call and is the only case that still escalates to lead. Failure modes with recovery paths are tabled in the review: silent half-regression (unfold on the count-0 row), cascade (the uncovered half is visible at claim time via its `*Acceptance:*`), loop (this entry is the standing rule), scope drift (folding-for-length refused, count is the tell).

## D244 — a seat's attention state is a named, owned state; idle (S2/S5/S6) may never reach the reset actuator, and a `pi.reset` record must carry its cause (2026-11-06; architect acting, queue #5211 / ROADMAP 313)

**Status.** Design accepted and in force as the contract for ROADMAP 314/316/317. Docs-only: **this entry changes no number and no knob** — it does not raise `DURIG_MAX_CONCURRENT_SEATS`, touch the verifier slot, or set a backoff value, per the operator's ordering ruling (D at `docs/DECISIONS.md:9489`: **backoff before capacity**, because every capacity knob multiplies the measured reset storm). Full table and failure modes: `docs/reviews/architecture-idle-attention-2026-11-06.md`.

**Context.** One bounded pass (`docs/ROADMAP.md:6006-6031`, `docs/SELFDEV.md:2234-2241`) recorded **`pi.reset 1,406`** against `pi.assistant 331` — the rig reset seats ~4x more often than it let them speak — with `escalated=1394`, `scribe:degeneration 592 / devtools 481 / pm 458`, ~**$0.17/h** of idle spend, and **31 resets to `lead`**, which erased an operator ruling from the only seat able to act on it. The cause is architectural, not a bad threshold: the rig has sensors for many conditions and **exactly two actuators** (reset, defer-to-human), and `planResets` (`src/supervisor.mjs:153-168`) fires purely on `assessment.degenerate`, so it cannot distinguish a quiet seat from a wedged one. `src/broker.mjs:1824-1836` then clears the seat's cooldown and marks the scheduler dirty, which is correct recovery for a wedged turn and an **accelerant** for idleness.

**Decision.** Eleven named states (S1 working … S11 paused), each with the `path:line` that owns its entry transition, what the rig does, who is woken, what is counted, and its wall-clock and counted-context cost — the table is in the review note and is the deliverable ROADMAP 313 asked for. One invariant, stated with an owner and a probe:
> **INV-1.** A `pi.reset` entry may exist only when a named per-run cause from S8 (wedged) or S9 (degenerate) is attached to it. An idle seat (S2 nothing-claimable, S5 parked, S6 gated) produces **zero** reset records.
Three defects block INV-1 today, each with an exact fix: **(1)** all 1,406 reset records carry **blank** text (`docs/SELFDEV.md:2241`) while the code does build a cause-named handoff (`src/supervisor.mjs:181-224`, written via `conv.reset(resetHandoff, …)` at `src/reset.mjs:70`) — so **stamp the cause on the reset record, not only in handoff prose**; **(2)** `assessRun` computes `justReset` (`src/degeneration.mjs:131-135`, returned `:231`) and **nothing consumes it** (probe: `grep -rn justReset src/ tools/ --include=*.mjs | grep -v '^src/degeneration.mjs'` → **0 lines**, measured), so the #1704 fix exists as a comment and a field but not as an act — make it load-bearing or delete it; **(3)** the live-generation-lease refusal is **conditional on a finite cap** (`src/reset.mjs:27-30`, consulted at `:54-55`; `maxSeatsFromEnv` → `Infinity` when `DURIG_MAX_CONCURRENT_SEATS` is unset, `:20-25`, measured `undefined`) so with the cap unset a reset can be drawn **under a running seat**, the one case its own header (`src/reset.mjs:11-13`) forbids — make the lease guard unconditional, since the cap sizes the pool and must not size the safety check.
Chosen shape: **wake-on-delta, not wake-on-pass** (option A), because the discriminator already exists (`SKIP reason=no-work`, `src/driver.mjs:111`) and the scheduler already has cooldowns and `markDirty` — it is a policy change, not a new sensor.

**Options considered.** **A. idle as a first-class scheduler state, wake on queue change** — chosen; reversible, single seam, makes 314/316/317 each "act on state X". **B. backoff timer only** — cheapest and reversible, but still pays a full prompt per wake, still leaves the reset path reachable from idleness, and re-tunes itself whenever capacity changes, which is the coupling the operator's ordering exists to break; acceptable only as an interim, and never with the guard able to fire on an empty queue. **C. raise the turn bound / relax the guard** — rejected: treats a symptom of the wrong edge, weakens the real S8/S9 protection, and cannot fix a blank reason record.

**Consequences.** (a) Idleness gets a cost line, not an actuator: S2/S5/S6 currently bill identically (one wake + one full prompt each), and 396 durable records in one 30-min pass carry the driver's no-work text (`docs/ROADMAP.md:6010`) — the rig paid ~400 times to be told there was nothing to do. (b) Every reset becomes attributable, so a pass report must print `resets=` beside `escalated=`; a blank reset record is by definition an attention bug, not capacity. (c) The recovery verbs split by state: reset for S8/S9 only, defer-to-human for S10, nothing at all for S2/S5/S6, restart-the-harness for S4. (d) A missed delta-wake is a new failure mode with a named backstop — the `admitted_not_started` notice (`src/attention.mjs:15-18`, `STRANDED_ADMITTED_MS = 30_000` at `:38`) is what makes S4 visible if the wake does not arrive. (e) A ruling must never live only in a seat's context: rulings ride as queue rows, because a legitimate S8 reset discards context and D-entries and rows survive. (f) The probes are **specified, not run**: no demo suite ran in this worktree (`vendor/pi-main` is unbuilt there, so a suite verdict would not be comparable with the seat root's). Acceptance stays ROADMAP 313's measured one — re-run the bounded pass on `queued 0`, require `escalations ≤ seat count` (not 1,394) and **zero `pi.reset` records**.

## D245 — the store close is the LAST act of the broker, not an independent one (INV-CLOSE); a closed store is a liveness failure, not a data-plane count (2026-11-06; architect, queue #5231 + addendum #5260; ROADMAP 303, sibling 327/329)

**Status.** Design accepted; **docs-only** — no code changed, and the four implementation seams are routed to `impl` via `pm`, not taken here. ADR number is **provisional**: re-mint at land time in issue order (the mint-at-land rule), never hardcode it in a branch. Full failure enumeration and probes: `docs/reviews/architecture-broker-linger-lifecycle-ordering-2026-11-06.md`.

**Context.** ROADMAP 303 is **5/5 reproduced** and the trigger is not the deadline and not the provider: pid 765129 took `STOP-REQUESTED source=file` → `EXIT pid=765129 reason=stop passes=15` at 09:35 and was still resident 13 minutes later (`docs/ROADMAP.md:6078`, `:6102`). The cost side is what raises severity: `selfdev.sqlite.broker.inbox.error/` holds **4 destroyed CLI reads** (`read health`, `read queue`), each `.reason` = `apply failed: SqliteStorage is closed` — a lingering broker holding a **closed** store does not merely delay the operator's reads, it deletes them. Reading the exit path named the fault: the broker enforces "never close the harness over a live run" (`src/broker.mjs:1978-1996`, F11) and has **no inverse guarantee** — store-close and loop-stop are two unlinked acts, so both orders are reachable and each degrades a different surface. Three ordered defects sit under it: **F1** `reopen()` closes both handles before it can guarantee a re-open (`cli.mjs:2055-2071`), so a failed open leaves the loop dereferencing a closed store; **F2** that failure is **invisible to every terminal counter** — `reopenCap` and `wakeRetryBudget` are entered only by a *thrown pass* (`src/broker.mjs:1871-1878`, `:1934`), while `drainIntentInbox` turns each apply failure into a dead-letter (`:782`) and the idle read drain turns it into a diagnostic and `continue`s (`:1713-1719`); **F3** the `.stop` **file** arms no force timer (`forceTimer` exists only inside `onSignal`, `cli.mjs:2094-2117`, reached from SIGINT/SIGTERM) and its drain is unbounded unless `stoppedBy === "deadline" || graceExpired()` (`src/broker.mjs:1992-1996`), while `serve --stop` explicitly refuses to escalate (`cli.mjs:1975-1988`) — so the operator's own verb cannot stop it, which is exactly the measured `serve --stop` → `kill` sequence. Adjacent drift: `cli.mjs:1948-1949` promises a 60 s wait; the code waits `resolveStopGraceMs() + 5_000` ≈ **10 s** (`:1956`, `STOP_GRACE_DEFAULT_MS = 5_000` at `:2006`).

**Decision.** **1. INV-CLOSE (the pairing that was missing).** *The store close is the last act of the process: after (i) the loop has stopped, (ii) every spooled intent is applied, dead-lettered with a reason, or re-queued, and (iii) no dereferenceable handle points at a closed store. Nothing that can execute an intent runs after close; if the close itself hangs, the process still exits within the force bound.* **2. On the #5260 ruling question — keep the store open and refuse to linger; do NOT fail closed on reads.** At the deadline the broker stops *accepting* intents with a named refusal (`broker-stopping` + pid + remaining grace), **fails-or-requeues** the pending inbox (this is ROADMAP 329's "an op enqueued during shutdown is stranded forever, silently" — same fault from the queue side, so it is folded into this row, not a new one), and keeps answering reads until the instant of close. **The control/write surface degrades on purpose; the read surface never does**, because 303's own measured lesson is that the store is the truth and the broker is a router that can go dark while alive (direct read-only open: **111 ms**; every broker-routed read: 120 s timeout). **3. A store-state failure is a LIVENESS failure.** A dead-letter whose reason is a store-state class (`closed`, `SessionFailed`) counts in `unactionedFailure` and can end the run terminally (`stoppedBy="store-unrecoverable"`) — never again an unbounded streak of error files with a fresh heartbeat. **4. Every stop path gets a force bound**, the `.stop` file included, and a forced exit reports the real completed-pass count and stop source (row 328's `passes=-` is the same defect seen in the record). **5. Liveness must be pid-attributed.** `heartbeatAt` may **accept** "some broker is alive" and may never **DECIDE** "this pid is working" (#3575 applied to this instrument): `brokerHealth`'s liveness leg (`src/broker.mjs:2131-2141`) reports the pid it read, and the 303/314 verdict requires a pid match — in the 09:35–09:48 window a second broker had already started, so the "fresh heartbeat" attributed to pid 765129 is ambiguous evidence. **6. 303 and 327 stay separate rows with separate conditions**: 303 is **refusal-to-exit**, 327 is **marker survival**. Clearing the stop file on exit does nothing for a broker that never reaches its exit path; bounding the drain does nothing for a request written into a run that has not started. Anyone tempted to fix both with one condition re-breaks the other.

**Options considered.** **A. Pair close with exit + bound every stop path + terminal counters** — chosen: reversible, three small seams, keeps the read surface honest; cost is a longer, explicitly-reported shutdown. **B. Fail closed on reads past the deadline** — rejected as primary: it converts a diagnosable dark-read window into an intentional one, indistinguishable from a broken store, and destroys facts rather than delaying them; admissible only as an add-on after A. **C. An outside watchdog kills the wedged pid** — cheapest, but the wrong owner: it forces the `passes=-` record, is the path that leaves a stop request behind for the next run (327), and destroys the in-flight evidence; accepted only as the last layer with a bounded grace.

**Consequences.** (a) "Linger" splits into two states that must not be merged: **L-A** resting on closed handles (destroys intents — the 4 dead-letters prove the loop was running) and **L-B** resident after `EXIT` with the store already closed (dark reads only; a ref'd keepalive at `src/scheduler.mjs:198-207` is unclosed, and `src/` holds only two `unref()` sites, `broker.mjs:1647`, `genlock.mjs:225`); they are told apart by `heartbeatAt` freshness **plus a pid match**. (b) A stopping broker becomes *legibly* unavailable — a named refusal instead of a timeout — so `status`/`health`/`queue` stay readable during shutdown and the wrong remedy (a write against a healthy store) stops being tempting. (c) Escalation becomes safe to add: with INV-CLOSE honoured, a forced exit no longer strands in-flight intents, which is what makes 329's fail-or-requeue the precondition for 303's bound rather than an unrelated row. (d) Every probe in the review is **RED-first** and two are already pinned by a green baseline: `node demo/broker-cooperative-stop.test.mjs` → **exit 0** in this worktree, which proves the gap is not stop *semantics* but the missing force bound — the fix must extend that file, not add a new one. (e) No new roadmap row is opened by this review; the four seams (F1 reopen atomicity, F2 counters, F3 force bound + `passes=` reporting, 329 requeue) and the pid-attribution leg are routed to `impl`/314 via `pm`.

---

## D246 — a spooled request has a LIFECYCLE: exit must fail-over the inbox residue, and a read is routed on PROGRESS, not liveness (#5275 / ROADMAP 329)

**Status:** Accepted (design). Build not yet landed — implementation routed to `impl` via `pm`; the `check`-rule half
goes to `devtools`. D-number minted at land time in issue order (lead #3075/#3186), never hardcoded here.

**Context.** The intent spool (`<db>.broker.inbox`) has no lifecycle: `drainIntentInbox` runs only at the start of a
pass (`src/broker.mjs:1243-1249`) or in the idle read-only branch (`1712-1727`), and `runWakeLoop`'s exit path
(`1984-2000`) never visits the inbox. Three shapes were observed: (a) a drain running against a closed
`SqliteStorage` → dead-letter `apply failed: SqliteStorage is closed`; (b) a drain not running → the read hangs with
no named cause (`watch --once --human`, 0 bytes on both streams, 90+ s); (c) an op enqueued during shutdown →
**stranded forever, silently** — no answer, no `.error.json`, and the next run's answer is written to a result slot
the caller already deleted (`src/readclient.mjs:49`). Measured at clock-in
(`node tools/stranded-inbox.mjs <repo>/selfdev.sqlite`, 2026-11-07T03:52Z): `inbox=7 shutdownStranded=0
drainStranded=7 hbAgeS=6 progressAgeS=2223 runSinceExit=yes` — five `read` and **two `message`** intents pending
against a broker whose heartbeat was 6 s old and whose last completed pass was 37 min old. So the limbo state is
reachable **without any shutdown**, and the routing boolean that sends a read there is `readData` →
`brokerAliveFor` → `brokerAlive` (`src/readclient.mjs:109-110`, `src/broker.mjs:2097-2106`), which is pid + heartbeat
only — the liveness-vs-progress conflation #5231/#5260 document, while `brokerHealth` (`src/broker.mjs:2138-2160`)
already computes the progress leg.

**Decision.**
1. **Exit is a transaction over the spool.** Before `clearBrokerState` and before the harness closes: one final
   `drainIntentInbox` bounded by the remaining grace (the #2420 `settleWithin` shape), then `deadLetterIntent`
   (`src/broker.mjs:239-259`) every still-pending entry with `broker exited (reason=<stoppedBy>) before this intent
   was drained`. That rides the channel `readIntentError`/`awaitIntentResult` already poll
   (`286-328`); no new channel.
2. **FAIL-with-named-cause is the default; requeue is the exception.** A replayed `read` answers about a session that
   no longer exists and lands in a slot its caller deleted; the duplicate-delivery family (#3087, #3877,
   impl-item-3192 / entry #3460) is the cost of re-enqueueing anything the caller may have retried. Requeue is
   reserved for ops carrying an epoch tag the next run can dedupe.
3. **One epoch primitive: `runToken`.** `writeBrokerState` already mints it per broker run
   (`src/broker.mjs:2217-2218`). 329(c) (entry survival) and 327 (#5258, marker survival) share it; do not introduce
   two ad-hoc "is this from the old run" conditions.
4. **Reads are routed on `brokerHealth(state).state`, not `brokerAlive`.** Three-way table: `up` → spool;
   `degraded` (pid alive, heartbeat fresh, no pass within the progress bound) → **refuse with
   `broker-degraded-no-progress`**, neither spool nor open the store; `down` (state gone, or
   `brokerProcessAlive` says the pid is gone, `2194-2204`) → `readLocal`, the caller is the sole owner. A client-side
   fallback to a direct store open while a writer lives stays **prohibited** (`src/readclient.mjs:3-11, 61-72`).
5. **The read's bound must be below the caller's patience**, derived from the progress bound rather than the
   hand-picked 120 s (`src/readclient.mjs:34`); a cause that arrives after the caller left is functionally silence.
6. **The population becomes a measure.** `tools/stranded-inbox.mjs` exits non-zero iff entries outlived the run that
   received them; a stale `broker.json` naming a dead pid becomes a check finding
   `broker-state-pid-not-running` (`status`/`check`), because that stale state is itself a *cause* of shape (b).

**Options considered.** (A) above — chosen: small, reversible, uses only existing channels, and makes the residue
countable. (B) *requeue everything for the next epoch* — cheapest at exit, rejected: it manufactures the stale-read and
duplicate-delivery classes it is meant to avoid, and makes the next broker's first pass semantically load-bearing on
work it was never asked to do. (C) *move the spool lifecycle into the store* (per-entry status/claim/lease, `dark`
in-database) — the right destination if (c) recurs after (A), rejected now: it needs the store open at the moment the
store is closing, and it widens the single-writer boundary far beyond the defect.

**Consequences.** Operator reads become **unavailable-and-loud** during a wedge instead of slow-and-silent; that is
the accepted price, since a refused read has a recovery path and a never-answering read does not. `brokerAlive` stays
legitimate for *identity* and for pid-death questions — but any consumer asking "can this broker answer me?" must call
`brokerHealth`, so call-sites that today use `brokerAlive` as a routing gate are on notice. `degraded` is now a state
with teeth, so a rig that shows it must be acted on (restart or repair), and the progress bound
(`DEFAULT_PASS_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000` + margin, `src/broker.mjs:2126-2155`) becomes a user-visible promise about read
latency. Acceptance is by probe, not by ordering argument: a demo that enqueues **mid-shutdown**, the mid-pass
closed-storage specimen, the `watch --once` non-zero-with-cause assertion, and
`tools/stranded-inbox.mjs` reporting zero shutdown-stranded entries on a live rig after a restart.

## D247 — 2026-11-08T08:2xZ: a parked-only seat is woken once per change of its parked set, not once per cooldown

**Decision (proposed, #5740; number minted at land time per #3075).** The wake contract for a seat whose only
non-terminal rows are `held` or `deferred` is: **wake when that seat's parked set changes**. `selectWakes`
(`src/driver.mjs:107`, the `hasParked` branch introduced by #4607) keeps its branch, and the broker supplies the
seat's last-known parked signature — the sorted set of `(itemId, status)` for that seat's parked rows — firing the
parked wake only when the signature differs. The signature lives on `WakeScheduler` (created once in `cmdServe`,
`cli.mjs:2023-2025`), not in `selectWakes`, which stays pure so the rule is demo-assertable.

**Context, measured.** Three runs against a throwaway single-seat rig, `DURIG_PROVIDER=faux`, counts from
`<db>.broker.log`, all exit 0: one held row + `serve --max-duration 120` → **4** wakes, at +0/+30/+60/+90 s;
two held rows + 60 s → **2** wakes; no queue rows + 60 s → **0**. The cadence is exactly
`SERVE_SEAT_COOLDOWN_MS = 30_000` (`cli.mjs:2688`). The wake's own submission is a commit that
`isWakeRelevantCommit` (`src/scheduler.mjs:44`) counts, and the cooldown-suppressed candidate schedules
`cooldownRevisitAt`, so the seat re-wakes itself with no external activity. The count is per seat, not per row.

**Alternatives considered.** (B) drop the parked wake and surface parked state as an attention kind — fewer turns,
but `src/attention.mjs` has no kind for a park, so the state becomes invisible rather than quieter. (C) a wake that
does not trigger a run — the cleanest semantics, unavailable: a submitted user entry drives a task in the pinned
pi-durable, and adding a non-running input is an upstream change. (A) was chosen because it is one predicate plus
one field, reversible, and preserves the informative wake #4607 exists to deliver.

**Consequences.** Accepted: a seat may hold stale knowledge of its parked set if nothing changed — it is one
`peek_queue` call away from refreshing it, and the wake would have carried no new information anyway. Rejected:
the unbounded alternative, which spends a seat turn every 30 s per parked seat, contends with the single
generation slot under the shipped `DURIG_MAX_CONCURRENT_SEATS: 1`, erodes the meaning of a wake, and never
converges. Suppression must be legible: `PARKED-WAKE seat=<n> reason=<set-changed|deduped>`, and the existing
`WAKE ${name}` line (`src/broker.mjs:1798`) must carry `reason=<queued|stalled-claim|parked>` — today it does not,
