## D248 — 2026-11-09T07:0xZ: a landing pass **composes** a journal conflict and mints the D-number at land time; it never picks a side in the shared tree (delegate acting on the operator's "run the landing pass now"; host measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v && git --version` → **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**, `git version 2.56.0`)

**What was decided.** When `scripts/land.mjs` reports a conflict in an append-only journal — `docs/DECISIONS.md`,
`docs/SELFDEV.md`, `docs/NEXT.md`, a runbook — the resolution is a **union**: main's already-landed content stays,
the branch's new entry is appended, and any placeholder or stale number the branch carried is **minted at land time**
from the next free slot in the ledger. Where the branch proposes code for a behaviour `main` already ships, main's
version wins and the branch's test is rewritten to assert the shipped shape.

**Why this and not "choose one side".** Three facts measured in the pass. (1) `scripts/land.mjs` merges in a scratch
detached worktree and advances `main` only by a clean fast-forward, so a conflict is a *stop*, not an accident: it
prints `STOPPED: 'item-5400' conflicts (demo/syncpi.test.mjs, scripts/sync-pi.mjs). The merge lives in the scratch
worktree — the SHARED tree was never touched and is not mid-merge`. Choosing a side in the shared tree would break
the invariant the gate exists to protect. (2) Journal entries are not alternatives; they are records. `item-5400` is
the proof: `#5094`'s pin-ref/drift fields and `#5282`'s read-back measurement are both real features, and picking one
would have deleted a shipped capability — the composed file passes `demo/syncpi.test.mjs` (PIN OK, LINK SPECS OK,
MALFORMED PIN OK, INSPECT OK). (3) Branch-carried D-numbers are **not** trustworthy: `item-5208`'s branch heading said
`D221`, and `main` had already minted `D221` for a different decision; `item-5211` carried `D224`/`D225` while `D224`
was taken. Minting at land time from the free slots (this pass: **D234, D242–D247**) is the only rule that cannot
collide, and it is why `item-4846`'s `D-<mint>` placeholder resolves rather than duplicates.

**Consequences.** A pass that stops on a conflict is not a failure of the pass; it is the gate doing its job, and the
delegate's job becomes composition in a scratch tree, then re-running `land.mjs`. Because landings change `main`, the
preflight must be re-run **inside** the loop (pitfall 173) and a composition can go stale mid-pass — `item-5740`'s
merge commit literally reads "re-composed on attempt 1 because main moved while the pass ran". Ancestor branches are
not merge targets: `item-5824` ⊂ `item-5740`, `item-5758` ⊂ `item-5663`, `item-5615` ⊂ `item-5712`, so landing the
superset makes the ancestors prunable, not landable.

**Boundary.** This rules on journal and doc conflicts and on code where main already ships the behaviour. It does
**not** authorise a delegate to close queue rows: the six landed-but-non-terminal rows (#5362, #5491, #5501, #5699
deferred; #5820 claimed; #5912 held) stay with their owners. And a stale base remains a re-cut job for the author
seat (`docs/runbooks/land.md` Do 0b) — `wip/seat-prompt-files` is left for its author, not merged by the delegate.

**Probe that falsifies it.** `git log --format='%s' main | grep -c '^merge: main into'` counts composed merges; `grep -c '^<<<<<<<' docs/DECISIONS.md` must be **0** after a pass; and `git merge-tree --write-tree main refs/heads/<branch>` must produce a tree identical to `main` for every branch whose patch is already applied (`git cherry` prints only `-`).

   175: the prompt section is static), and a `beforeCompact` hook on `CompactionTask` that supplies the summary

   200 non-terminal rows instead of 6,021, and ships `queueCensus` (rows, per-state counts, terminal/active),
   `queueDeferred` (every deferred row's id, seat, status and a 55-char subject) and, on request,
   `queueTerminalIndex` (ids+statuses of the dropped rows). `peerGraph` is derived from the rows actually shown,
   and `graphOmittedEdges` names what is not there. `--full-queue` on a store over the cap **exits 1 with the
   count** instead of hanging the read.

**Why this and not "just cap the output".** The measurement: `node cli.mjs status --json` on this rig printed

bound the same command prints **587,109 bytes** (`queueItems` 389,829, `queueDeferred` 51,353, `peerGraph` 49,315,
`queueCensus` 133). The first cut of the bound **broke clock-in silently**: `scripts/clockin.mjs (`runCli(["status"])` in `main`)` runs
`runCli(["status"])` for its queue section, so a 200-row view made the digest print `## QUEUE 200 rows` and a
**zero** deferred backlog against a store holding 383 rows awaiting the operator. Nothing else in the suite looked
at that line against a production-shaped store, so 280 demos stayed green while the entry point lied. The rule is
now enforced by code and by a demo: `demo/status-view-bound.test.mjs` seeds a 400-row store (100 terminal, 250
deferred — more deferred rows than the cap) and asserts the census and the full deferred backlog travel, that the
index is opt-in and body-free, and that `droppedTerminal + droppedCapped === total − shown`.

**Consequences.** Any new read verb that projects a document must answer three questions in its payload: how many
rows exist, which rows it dropped and why, and what size it saved. A derived number (census, attention, graph)
that a reader could recompute only from the full row set must be computed before projection and shipped — the

row count equal to its shown count on a store larger than the cap, the rule has regressed.

### Addendum, same session — a boundary the seat did not choose

The note reached a seat only when the seat asked for it (`read_note`, `continue_from_note`) or when a compaction
used it as its summary. `cli.mjs reset <seat>`, `up --refresh` and the degeneration guard all call
`conversation.reset(handoff)` **with no handoff** (`src/reset.mjs:59-60`, `dist/harness/harness.js:45`), so a
seat woken into a fresh context still started from nothing — the exact symptom D240 exists to close.
`extensions/continuity.mjs` now registers a `beforeRequest` hook on `GenerationTask`: when the visible
projection is short (≤ 2 non-system messages) and the note text is not already in it, the note is appended to
the **system message** of the next request. Three rulings inside that choice:

- **System message, not a new turn.** `tools/seat-turn-shape.mjs` measured **9 of 12** live seats already
  carrying consecutive user turns; adding a `user` turn is the shape a strict alternating chat template
  refuses, and it would trade a window problem for a shape problem.
- **Bounded by construction, not by apology.** Injection stops as soon as the seat has its own context back, so
  the note is a boundary mechanism rather than a per-request tax (ROADMAP 175). The injected block is stable
  while the note is unchanged, so the cached prefix is not churned.
- **It is not durable, and must not pretend to be.** The hook replaces the request only
  (`dist/harness/generation.js:118-123`); the transcript gains no entry. The durable record of a note is the
  `durig.notes` document, and a gate that looked for the injected text in `entries` would find nothing and
  conclude the mechanism failed.

**Also in this addendum:** the milestone gate now separates *mechanism* failures (exit 1) from *operational*
blockers (no broker, no key, extension unlisted) and *advisory* risk signals. Measured 2026-11-09: PASS
(mechanism) on `./selfdev.sqlite` with 8 operational blockers, and PASS (mechanism) on the armed demo store
with 1. `node demo/continuity-note.test.mjs` → `CONTINUITY PASS`, 0.630 s, five scenarios.

## Pending (D-number minted at land time, per the convention at line 3233) — **a read routes on HEALTH, not on LIVENESS, and the diagnostic surface must survive the refusal** (architect, item #5631, 2026-11-10)

**Status.** DESIGN OF RECORD for RM-329 2/3 + 3/3. Not yet implemented; no code is changed by this entry.

**Context.** `brokerHealth` (`src/broker.mjs:2239`) already computes `up | degraded | down` from two legs —
LIVENESS (heartbeat + pid) and PROGRESS (`lastPassAt` within `streamTimeout + BROKER_PROGRESS_MARGIN_MS`) —
but only `status` prints it. `readData` (`src/readclient.mjs:109-111`) routes on `brokerAliveFor`, liveness
alone, with `timeoutMs = 120_000` (`:35`). Measured in an item worktree of main `f192f543`
(`node tools/probes/routing-on-liveness-vs-progress.mjs`, exit 0): a live pid, a fresh heartbeat and a
6-hour-old `lastPassAt` sends a `queue` read to the spool (inbox 0 → 1) and the caller waits out the
literal — exit ETIMEDOUT at 40 s, the same shape the live store shows now (`inbox=9 drainStranded=9
resultFiles=0 hbAgeS=5 progressAgeS=22731`). A state naming a DEAD pid already routes to `readLocal` and
answers in 373 ms, so the `down` leg is not the gap.

**Decision.** One predicate, one verdict, two consumers. (1) `brokerAlive` keeps the heartbeat-stale guard
and calls `brokerProcessAlive` rather than carrying its own `process.kill(pid, 0)` block — the same
`!== "ESRCH"` fail-safe (#3398) written twice in one file is the drift the row is hunting for. (2) `readData`
computes `brokerHealth` once and routes three-way: `up` → spool; `degraded` → structured refusal
(`code = "broker-degraded-no-progress"`, `err.db`, the ages in the message) that touches **neither the
spool nor the store**; `down` → `readLocal`, and "proven gone" means the conjunction of a fresh-enough
heartbeat and `ESRCH`, never signal 0 alone. (3) The read bound is **derived** — `min(progressTimeoutMs,
callerBound)`, 10-30 s default — replacing the 120 s literal, and the number is named in the demo. (4) The
3/3 check rule reads `<db>.broker.json` off-store and calls the same predicate; it must survive an
unreadable store.

**Consequences.** `status`, `queue`, `check` and every read verb inherit one definition of "is the broker
useful right now", so a seat and an operator cannot get different answers from two surfaces. Refusal is
fast and named, which is what makes a permanent refusal survivable rather than a reason to kill the process.
The cost is real and must be designed for: if `degraded` refuses reads, the operator's way of SEEING the
wedge is itself refused — measured, 40 s, ETIMEDOUT — so `status` must answer inside the bound with the
broker block and the store-derived sections marked unavailable, not error out. Demos must refresh the
forged heartbeat before each verb or they pass for the wrong reason: the 60 s liveness gate
(`BROKER_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `src/broker.mjs:2195`) makes a once-forged state read as dead by the third
call (#5829, recorded in `docs/runbooks/broker-down-or-stalled.md`); this probe hit exactly that trap on
its first run.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) Lower the bound only, keep liveness routing — cheap, one literal; rejected
as a sole fix because the caller still gets a timeout with no cause and the spool still accumulates
undrained intents. (b) On `degraded`, fall back to `readLocal` — rejected outright: it puts a second writer
against a broker that is alive, and `SqliteStorage.document()` takes `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` even for a read;
"unavailable-and-LOUD" is the ruling. (c) Route on signal-0 liveness for simplicity — rejected: a recycled
pid or a broker mid-pass is misclassified, and a false-dead report admits the second writer that corrupted
run-control docs twice on 2026-10-16.

## D258 — a push-batch boundary is MEASURED AT GRANT TIME by the executor; an intake count nobody can re-check is labelled UNVERIFIED and never sets the boundary (lead #5626; recorded by scribe, item #5668, 2026-11-10)

**Mint note (#3075/#3186 discipline).** Minted at land time as **D258**: the landing pass derived the next FREE
number by scanning this file at merge (`grep -oE '^## D[0-9]+' docs/DECISIONS.md | sort -n | tail -1` → D257 on
main at merge). The branch hardcodes no number and reserves none.

**Decision.** A push grant's batch boundary is read off the tree **at grant time, by whoever executes the grant**:
`git rev-list --count <last-granted-tip>..HEAD`, cross-checked against `git log --oneline`, and the grant names
the ending tip sha. Three consequences follow:
1. A count quoted at intake by a seat with no shell or file surface is **UNVERIFIED**, must be labelled as such,
   and may never set the boundary.
2. The boundary is **not** pre-measured by another seat earlier in the session. It goes stale at the next land,
   and a stale boundary is precisely how a later push attempt meets a refusal nobody predicted.
3. Landed-but-unpushed history is un-counted debt in the shared checkout. The measurement is not bookkeeping —
   it is the prediction.

**Measured 2026-11-10 in this item's worktree off `f192f543` (every command exit 0):**
- `git rev-parse --verify origin/main` → `1b985538`.
- `git rev-list --count origin/main..main` → **23**: main is 23 commits ahead of the pushed tip. That is the debt
  the rule is about, in a number anyone can re-run.
- `git rev-list --count f192f543..HEAD` → **1**: this branch's own batch, measured by the seat that produced it,
  with the ending tip named in the commit.
No push was attempted or implied: push capability is held by the operator (no `DURIAN_PI_ALLOW_PUSH` grant in
this session), and an entry is a rule, not a grant.

**What this is an instance of.** The rig's own rule — a cheap signal may ACCEPT but must never DECIDE — applied
to operator-side grants. The principle is carried in `docs/BRANCH-AND-WORKTREE-LIFECYCLE.md:228` and
`docs/reviews/worktree-seat-state-resolution-2026-11-06.md:145`. Say plainly what is missing: **#3575 has no
DECISIONS entry**, so a reader following a "#3575" cross-reference lands on a queue row, not a ruling. Cite the
doc; keep the row id as provenance only.

**Disposition of the two rows this came out of, because the next seat will ask.**
- The fresh **D218** push grant IS an operator-level digest row: it postdates the operator's nine-row cut
  (D234 §2(iii)) and needs the operator's ack to be in scope. pm did not silently override ruling (iii); the
  row says so in its own heading.
- **`cap=3 gated on #5488` is NOT a digest row.** Its premise went false when the operator ruled the standing
capacity option **approved-gated**: land #5488 first, then raise to the 3 measured slots (`total_slots: 3`,
`n_ctx 204800`, `qwen3.8-flash-next-iq3_s`, re-measured at 00:26Z) — D234 §3(i). **Update, measured here: that
condition is now satisfied.** `git merge-base --is-ancestor f4554164 main` and `git merge-base --is-ancestor
cfef4d07 main` both exit 0 (`f4554164 fix(cli, #5488): DURIG_MAX_CONCURRENT_SEATS gates the local/* providers
too`; `cfef4d07 test(demo, #5488 #5736): prove the cap BITES at 4`), and the gate is live in the code at
`src/config.mjs:120,631` and `src/reset.mjs:21`. The D233 gate must therefore not be reopened on the grounds
that #5488 is unlanded — it is landed. There is no gap between the two rows: one is in scope pending an ack, the
other is out of scope because its premise died.

**This entry does not depend on the digest carrier.** The carrier for the operator digest is **#5598** (scribe,
gated on **#5594**), still deferred as of this recording, and D234 §2(iii) says its body must be re-pointed at
the FOUR standing asks before anything is printed. Nothing here cites a digest section that does not exist yet.

**Verify (ran; exit codes named).** `node tools/doc-integrity-guard.mjs` → 0 hard, 0 soft, exit 0.
`docs/NEXT.md` was NOT touched by this entry and stands at **143 lines / 11,671 bytes** — inside the 200-line /
~17 KB carrier bound the verify step asks about. `docs/DECISIONS.md` is **11,161 lines** at the fork point.

## D259 — a not-yet-landed SPEC document constrains LAND ORDER, never START; a self-addressed successor row is routed through the intake seat (lead #5628; recorded by scribe, item #5678, 2026-11-10)

**Mint note (#3075/#3186 discipline).** `D###` is a placeholder on purpose; the landing pass derives the next
FREE number by scanning this file at merge. Highest at this branch's fork point `f192f543` is **D256** —
re-derive, do not assume 257.

**Rule 1 — a dangling SPEC is an ordering constraint, not a gate.** When a build item cites a document that is
not yet on main: the document is merged **below** the build tips that cite it (its D-number re-minted at land
time), and **the build proceeds**. It is NOT made a `blockedBy` on the build work. Two reasons, both measured
elsewhere in the record:
- Gating running work on a docs land is the gate-starvation family. `docs/reviews/security-5269-landing-correction.md:103-104`
  lists three instances in one session of "a gate bound to the wrong object": #3747 (a gate naming a cancelled
  id), #3863 (a gate bound to a cancelled twin), #5269 (a gate clause bound to the wrong thing). A gate keyed on
  a document that has not landed is the same shape with a different object.
- It duplicates a mechanism that already works. `docs/runbooks/land.md:116` carries lead's principle verbatim:
  **DEPENDENCIES ARE ENFORCEABLE AND ORDERING REQUESTS ARE NOT.** The landing lock is enforceable; an ordering
  request is not. "When a gate duplicates a mechanism, the mechanism wins and the gate goes."

**Companion rule — label a dangling citation; never silently re-point it.** A seat that finds a citation to a
document not on main writes it in its own completion as **UNVERIFIED / not-on-main**, with the command that
showed it. It does not re-point the citation at a branch tip. The reason is the evidence-tree rule the rig
already runs (`src/checkup.mjs:115`, rule id `evidence-tree`): a check must name the tree it ran against, and
re-pointing a citation at an unlanded tip changes the tree silently, which is exactly what makes a green
unverifiable.

**Rule 2 — the self-edge refusal is the rule working, not a schema gap.** `SEND_WORK_ERROR: org edge forbids
architect -> architect` is the intended behaviour. `src/rig.mjs:73-85` throws whenever the target is not in the
sender's declared `maySendTo`. Measured in this worktree off `f192f543` (exit 0):
`node -e "require('./rig.selfdev.json').edges.forEach(l=>console.log(l.from, l.maySendTo.includes(l.from)))"`
prints **false for all 12 edge rows** — no seat lists itself, by construction. So successor rows for a seat are
registered **through the intake seat (pm)**, which is where the `blockedBy` gates and held rows live. A genuinely
needed self-edge is an operator-level schema ask, never a seat-side workaround.

**What is NOT instrumented, stated so the entry is not read as a control.** Merge order is a pass-branch
practice, not a checked property: `grep -niE "land order|merge order|below the build" docs/runbooks/land.md
docs/runbooks/merge.md` returns nothing, and nothing in `tools/` or `scripts/` enforces doc-below-build
ordering. The rule is recorded here and mirrored into the landing runbook so the next pass has a procedure
rather than an anecdote.

**Family, cited not restated.** The principle behind rule 1 — a cheap signal may ACCEPT but must never DECIDE —
is carried in `docs/BRANCH-AND-WORKTREE-LIFECYCLE.md:228`; note that **#3575 has no DECISIONS entry**, so the
row id is provenance, not a citable ruling. Same for **#3252** (provider/model moves are operator-level): that
entry exists only on the unlanded branch `item-3252` (tip `4174ecc`), so it is not yet on main and must not be
cited as if it were.

**Verify (ran; exit codes named).** `node tools/doc-integrity-guard.mjs` → 0 hard, 0 soft, exit 0. The edge
measurement above, exit 0. `docs/DECISIONS.md` is 11,161 lines at the fork point; `docs/NEXT.md` is untouched
by this entry at 143 lines / 11,671 bytes.

## D260 — checkpointing is per-doc and bounded by cadence, not by the verb that caused the change (architect, item #6171, ROADMAP 355 A, 2026-11-10)

**Status.** Proposed ruling; number minted at land time (the mint-at-land rule, #3075). No code changed in this
row — `impl` implements it under its own row. Measurements and failure enumeration:
`docs/reviews/architecture-checkpoint-policy-2026-11-10.md`, probe
`docs/evidence/2026-11-10-checkpoint-policy/probe.mjs` (pi-durable **1.3.0** as resolved by the lockfile, node
v24.22.1, branch `item-6171`; run: `node docs/evidence/2026-11-10-checkpoint-policy/probe.mjs 5000 10000`, exit 0).

**Context.** `defineDoc`'s `checkpointWhen(value, ops, info)` decides whether a change is stored as a full base
or a delta; reads replay every delta since the nearest base (`dist/storage/sqlite/storage.js:426-450`), and for
session-scoped (current-only) docs writing a base **deletes** the prior revisions (`storage.js:652,655`). The rig
put `() => false` on all six docs as a provisional stop for the pin move. The intake asked for the predicate to be
keyed on the transitions a reader acts on (claim, complete, defer, hold, release) — for the queue doc that set is
*every mutation*, so taken literally it is `() => true`, which measured 50× worse: 10,000 queue verbs cost
30,703 ms checkpointing every verb against 608 ms checkpointing none.

**Decision.** Four policies, by doc shape and read cadence:
- `RigQueue` (5,077 rows, ~2 MB, read by `watch` every ~750 ms and twice per broker pass, `src/broker.mjs:214,1258,1339`): `info.deltasSinceBase >= 200` — cadence, not verb class. Measured at 10,000 verbs: read 5.38 ms vs 12.29 ms with no checkpoints, for 21 base writes (+148 ms). A tighter bound (50) costs 46% more write time for no measured read gain.
- `Seats`, `Edges`, `Constitution`, `RigControl` (session singletons, tiny, read on every wake/send/prompt build, changed rarely): `() => true`. Small-doc probe: 200 writes cost 36.6 ms with a base each time vs 42.3 ms with none.
- `ContinuityNotes` (conversation-scoped, `history: "rewindable"`, `fork: "asOf"`): `info.deltasSinceBase >= 20`. History is retained for conversation docs, so a base is an add, not a replacement; the bound bounds replay depth and history growth at once.
- Every rig doc must declare a predicate. `() => false` is not neutral: at the pin it is silently skipped, at `v1.5.1` a missing predicate throws (`session/transaction.ts:1058`, the 3 demo failures in the delta review).

**Consequences.** Reads become predictable rather than merely usually fast; a decision-gating doc (queue →
landing readiness via `LANDING_QUEUE_STATUSES`, `src/readapi.mjs:673`; control → wake; seats → claim) no longer
invites a cache, because its read is bounded. Nobody can read an old queue state out of a session doc — that
history never existed (`isCurrentOnly`, `storage.js:57`), and the audit trail is each item's `transitions` array.
The live-store size delta against the backup baseline (`617,492,480 bytes`, sha256 `0996cd61…`) is NOT measured
here, because that needs the live store and the read seam forbids a second opener; it belongs to the build row.
Failure modes with their probes are enumerated in the review (§5); the predicate contract (pure, total, O(1) over
`info`, no I/O) is §6.

## D261 — 2026-11-10T13:2xZ: **a row's authority is per-field: intent belongs to the two parties, gates belong to whoever mints them, and a constraint with no field is not a constraint** (architect ruling on pm's row #6225, "the coordinator has routing authority but not edit authority"; host measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v` → **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**)

**The why.** pm tried to attach a sequencing constraint to a row lead had minted, and had nowhere to
put it. The tempting fix — let the coordinator edit a routed row's body — answers the symptom and
leaves the cause standing. The cause is structural: `workable()` reads `item.blockedBy`
(`src/rig.mjs:310`) and never reads a sentence, so a constraint that cannot reach a field is not a
constraint at all. Measured with `tools/probes/revise-authority-boundary.mjs` (exit 0, worktree
`item-6185` @ `f192f543`, faux provider, `MemoryStorage`): the coordinator's `revise_work` is
refused; the *sender's* `revise_work` carrying `blockedBy` is dropped at schema validation, and the
body edit riding in the same call is dropped with it; `workable()` on a gate naming a nonexistent id
returns `{workable: true}`. `blockedBy` is assigned in exactly one place, `enqueueItem`
(`src/rig.mjs:441`, reached only from `send_work` at `:737`) — there is no post-mint gate write path
for anyone.

**Decision.** Four boundaries, each falsifiable:

1. **Intent (`subject`, `body`): the two parties only, `queued` only.** Unchanged, and not widened.
   "The coordinator" is not a field on a row; `from` and `to` are. Authority the guard cannot derive
   from the record is authority it cannot enforce.
2. **Constraint (`blockedBy`, `requires`, `tier`, `block`): mint-scoped.** If you hold the gate, mint
   the row that carries it. `hold_work`'s recipient-only rule (`src/rig.mjs:1212`) is the one
   asymmetry worth removing: a minting seat can release and cancel its own row but cannot park it, so
   its only legal lever for a premature row is the terminal one. Parking must not be harder than
   cancelling.
3. **A future `gate_work` verb is additive-only for a non-minting party, authority = parties plus a
   *recorded* coordinator, `queued` only, and gated on validation first.** Adding a gate is
   reversible and conservative; removing one loosens a contract another seat authored, which is a
   scope ruling, not a verb. Validation precedes authority: `normalizeBlockedBy` (`src/rig.mjs:355-380`)
   checks shape only — it does not check that the id exists, is non-terminal, or is acyclic, and a
   dangling gate is inert while a cancelled one starves forever. Handing out gate-writing power before
   those checks turns a well-meaning coordinator into a starvation engine.
4. **Terminality is checked before authority in every control verb.** `release_work` learned this as
   #5778 (`src/rig.mjs:1254`); `revise_work` and `cancel_work` still answer "not yours to revise" for
   a row that is already `done`, which is how a fleet reports a closed row as open work.

**Consequences.** Coordinators gain a real path (mint with the gate, or ask a party to) instead of a
prose channel the claim predicate cannot see. Two defects are registered for repair: the `hold_work`
asymmetry, and the authority-before-terminality ordering in `revise_work`/`cancel_work`. The cost is
one extra hop per discovered constraint, plus a schema requirement — coordinator standing must be a
recorded field on the row before any verb can grant it. That schema decision is `lead`'s and is not
made here.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) widen `revise_work` to the routing seat — rejected: routing is not
recorded, so the guard would have to infer authority from role or the org graph. (b) keep the status
quo and let late constraints live in bodies — rejected: measured failure, 42 held rows in
`demo/queue-held-gates.test.mjs` carrying no recorded gate at all, and #6218 is the live specimen.
**Status:** adopted as a ruling on the boundary; the verb, the asymmetry fix and the ordering fix are
routed, not implemented here.

## D258 — 2026-11-10T13:5xZ: **enforcement at the receive path is structural admission; the audit sink is broker-written evidence, never a decision input; and a deny whose record cannot be written is a STUCK payload, not a dead-letter** (architect ruling on pm's row #6185, "what may enforce on the broker receive path, and who may write the audit sink"; host measured with `uname -s && uname -r && (. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME") && node -v` → **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**)

**The why.** The receive path is the one place a payload arrives from outside the broker, and every
control decision made there has to be both enforceable and legible. `authorizeSpoolRequest`
(`src/broker.mjs:505`) is the right shape: **pure**, no store, no harness, no model — so the rule is
testable with no broker (`demo/control-plane-gate.test.mjs`, exit 0). But three measured things show
the seam is not yet sealed.

**1. Admission runs on a defaulted discriminator.** `requestOp` returns `"message"` when `op` is
absent (`src/broker.mjs:469-471`). So a payload with no op is ALLOWED by the gate and only fails later
at seat lookup. A typo'd op is allowed by the gate and dead-lettered by the drain's `SPOOL_OPS` check
— opposite verdicts, two code paths, same payload. Enforcement on a value the parser invented is not
enforcement. **Decision:** an absent or unknown `op` is refused at the gate.

**2. A content-classifier deny at ingest would deny the rig's own evidence.** Measured with
`docs/evidence/2026-11-10-broker-receive-path/probe.mjs` (exit 0): 5 of 6 routine payloads — an
evidence sha, an ADR sha256, a worktree branch name, an npm lockfile hash, a real key — FIRE the
existing secret classifier as `high-entropy-token`. The only exemption that exists
(`src/gitobject.mjs`) is confirmation-based (`git cat-file -e`) and is a subprocess with a probe
budget. **Decision:** enforce on **structure** — op, actor, target, capability — never on content
shape. A gate that fires on shas is a gate you cannot turn on.

**3. The recovery leg lies about itself.** When `<db>.broker.inbox.error` exists as a *file*,
`deadLetterIntent` swallows the EEXIST (`src/broker.mjs:305-307`) and the caller still does
`deadLettered += 1` (`:791`, `:812`, `:856`). Measured: `pass1 deadLettered=1 … payload still in the
inbox after two passes: 1`, re-drained every pass with no cap — `INTENT_RETRY_LIMIT` bounds only the
closed-handle branch. An unparseable payload is dead-lettered with **no** diagnostic at all.
**Decision:** split the counters (`deadLettered` vs `stuck`), emit a diagnostic on every refusal
branch, and bound the stuck branch with the same attempt sidecar the retry path already uses.

**Who may write the audit sink.** Only the broker writes it today, and that is an accident of how a
command is spelled, not an authority: `src/confine.mjs` has zero hits for `audit`, `inbox` or `spool`;
`echo x >> <db>.broker.audit.log` is refused by the lexical guard, while the same write inside a
`node -e` program succeeds (measured; the probe line was removed immediately after the measurement).
**Options considered:** (a) name the sink paths in the guard — helps against shell redirection, nothing
against an interpreter; kept as a **layer**, not a boundary. (b) make authority come from the record's
provenance: the broker writes the decision it made against the spool file it decided on, and the
enforceable artifact is the structured `refusal` object on the dead-lettered record
(`src/broker.mjs:295-303`), cross-checkable against the `.reason` files and the recorded result.
**Adopted: (b), with (a) as a layer.** The trade-off named out loud: nothing may *act* on the audit log
— it is evidence only — which costs a cross-check at read time, in exchange for the decision being a
function of broker-held state rather than of a file any seat process can append to. This is the same
doctrine `authorizeSpoolRequest` already carries: `from` is producer-stamped, all seats share one OS
user, so same-user forgeability is a KNOWN RESIDUAL and must never be described as prevented.

## D259 — The fault signal is ONE seat-scoped marker written by the code that RAISES the cause, read as four states, and UNKNOWN never means "no fault" (2026-11-10)

**Status:** ruling issued (schema, not code); implementation routed and gated on this row.

**Context:** `workable()`'s contract has four clauses; three are implemented. Clause 4 — "not marked
blocked by a recorded PROVIDER/SEAT FAULT" — has no field, and D24 forbids inventing one. Measured by
`node tools/probes/fault-signal-states.mjs` (exit 0): **1 distinct verdict out of 6 fault situations** —
active, expired, unreadable and absent faults all read as "clean" — and an undeclared option passed to
the predicate is silently dropped, no error, no effect. Today the rig's only durable expression of a
fault is the supervisor's park on an item (`src/supervisor.mjs:75-92`), derived each pass from the
transcript: observation time, not fault time, no provenance, no expiry. That is why the gap has sat
parked since #2673.

**Decision:**
- **The marker is on the seat** (`Seats.seats[name].fault`), not the item. The live store measures 2,961
  queue items and 12 seats (`node cli.mjs config`); a fault is a property of the actor, and per-item
  marking would write and unwrite ~3k rows per outage.
- **Shape mirrors the park shape** (`normalizeBlock`, `src/queue-lifecycle.mjs:146`): `cause` from the
  `src/causes.mjs` allow-list, `scope`, `at` (fault time), `by` (the raiser), `evidence`, `resolver`
  (mandatory), `reviewBy` (mandatory — a fault with no expiry is permanent starvation). The write path
  refuses a marker missing any of them.
- **Only the raiser writes it, at fault time** — `src/providers/spend.mjs` for `SPEND_CAUSE`, the
  run-settle path for `model_error`, in the commit that settles the failing submission. `attention`,
  `checkup` and the supervisor are READERS; the supervisor stops deriving the fault in order to decide.
- **The read is four states:** `none`, `active`, `expired`, `unknown`. `workable()` gains a *named*
  `fault` parameter — naming is load-bearing, because an undeclared key is silently dropped today — and
  returns `reason: "fault:<cause>"` when active, keeping `reason: null` while carrying `caveats:
  ["fault-unknown" | "fault-expired:<cause>"]` otherwise, so the invariant "a non-null reason means not
  workable" survives.
- **UNKNOWN is claimable but never reported as clean.** #2673's conservative default is kept: a false
  negative starves invisibly, a false positive is legible. A broken fault read does not stop the claim;
  it names the state, prints it in the claim response, and is counted by `check`.
- **Clause 4 gates claim and wake through the same predicate** (`src/queue-lifecycle.mjs:348` already
  assigns claimability to `workable`), and gates nothing else — a seat mid-run must still be able to
  complete, defer, hold, release or resume.

**Options considered:** (a) `fault` on the item — cheapest to write, impossible to clear; (b) derive it
at claim time from the transcript — rejected: not persisted (D24), makes a provably pure predicate
impure, and uses observation time when the decision needs fault time; (c) one seat-scoped marker written
by the raiser — **chosen**.

**Consequences:** a write lands on the provider seam, the rig's hottest path; a bug there blocks claims
fleet-wide. Accepted because the decision is reversible both ways — clause 4 can be switched off without
touching the data, and the marker is independently auditable. Expiry is mandatory, so a fault cannot
become permanent starvation; a faulted seat that is never woken would never clear, so the wake selector
must wake a seat whose `reviewBy` has passed. `fault-unknown` is a countable finding, so "the fault check
is broken" is visible rather than looking like an empty queue.

**Residual:** this ruling fixes the shape and the read states. It does not decide which causes qualify,
nor whether a faulted seat should be re-tested before its expiry — that is a scope question for `lead`.

## D262 — 2026-11-10T23:0xZ: **a signal must abort the await, not set a flag; a read is bounded by the broker's PROGRESS, not its LIVENESS; and an interrupted verb exits 130** (delegate acting on the operator's goal "make every CLI verb answer or fail fast — no 120 s silence — and make Ctrl-C actually terminate the running command"; host measured with the measurement: **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**, `git version 2.56.0`)

**Status:** landed on `main` as `41000315` + `c32557cb` + `src/cli-seam.mjs`; nothing pushed.

**Context.** Every read verb ends in `awaitIntentResult(...)`, a poll that could run the full
120 s spool bound. The verbs that "handled" SIGINT (`watch`, `log`, `events`, `run --watch`,
`serve`) set `stopping = true` on a loop that was already inside an await — the handler fired, the
flag flipped, and the process kept sitting on the await it was already in. Measured on the
baseline `e06626af` with a forged resident-but-unanswered broker and a 139 KB store:
`cli.mjs watch --once --json` took **120,547 ms** and exited **1**, with the Ctrl-C landing
**119,043 ms** before the process gave up. `status` and `queue` had no handler at all and died by
node's default: 0 bytes, no exit code a caller can branch on. Evidence:
`docs/evidence/2026-11-10-cli-signals/ctrl-c-and-read-bounds.md`.

**Decision.**
- **One seam, not per-verb flags.** `src/signals.mjs` holds one process-wide `AbortController`.
  Every poll loop uses `stoppableSleep`; `awaitIntentResult` (`src/broker.mjs:363`) takes the
  signal and returns in one 200 ms poll. A repeat `installSignalHandlers` call can only RAISE the
  grace (verbs with a longer shutdown get it), never remove the handler.
- **The seam is installed by the first import.** `src/cli-seam.mjs` is `cli.mjs`'s first import,
  because in ESM a module body cannot run before its own imports resolve; measured registration at
  **271 ms** instead of ~500 ms. The remaining window is stated in the evidence doc rather than
  hidden: ESM cannot beat it without a separate entry file.
- **Exit code 130.** A verb interrupted while it was still working exits **130 (128 + SIGINT)**
  and prints `{ok:false, command, interruptedBy, stoppedBy:"signal"}`, even if it printed a full
  payload first. If the verb had already finished, 0 is the honest code — measured: `ps`
  SIGINT@400 ms on the baseline exited 0 because the verb was done.
- **The read bound is derived from PROGRESS, not LIVENESS.** `BROKER_READ_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000`
  while the broker is advancing (`src/readclient.mjs:40`); `DEGRADED_READ_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000`
  when the heartbeat is fresh but `lastPassAt` is frozen (`:43`). A resident broker that does not
  answer falls back to the store **only if no seat holds a live generation lease**
  (`liveGenerationLeases`, `:68`); otherwise it fails with a named cause
  (`broker_degraded` / `broker_read_timeout`) and the runbook remedy.
- **The safe direct read is read-only.** pi-durable cannot open a store read-only and takes
  `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for reads, so `src/readonlystore.mjs` (node:sqlite `readOnly`) is the only
  direct read that is safe next to a resident broker. `demo/readonly-store-parity.test.mjs` pins
  **15 views** byte-identical between pi-durable and the shim — including the ascending order
  `log --follow` polls, which the shim initially returned newest-first, silently dropping every
  entry between polls.
- **Reads are drained out of band.** `runWakeLoop` runs a read drain on the heartbeat cadence
  (`readDrainMs = 1_000`, `readDrainBoundMs = 10_000`, `src/broker.mjs:1670-1671`, timer at
  `:1799`), guarded three ways: only when every pending intent is a read, one drain at a time,
  and bounded so a wedged drain is logged (`READ-DRAIN-STUCK`) rather than held. Reads are served
  from the broker's second connection (`probeStorage`), never the harness handle that is stuck.

**Options considered:** (a) a timeout flag per verb — rejected, it is the bug being fixed;
(b) let any verb open the store directly when the broker is slow — rejected: a second owner
contending with a mid-generation seat is the corruption class the broker exists to prevent;
(c) one abort-aware seam plus a read-only shim — **chosen**.

**Consequences.** `Ctrl-C` latency is bounded by the blocking call in flight, not by a hard wall:
the force-exit timer can only fire when the event loop is free, and a multi-MB result read can
block it for seconds (measured ~2.5 s worst case). The result-channel GC
(`gcIntentResults`, `src/broker.mjs:417`, called per pass at `:1361`) is not on the read-drain
path, so a wedged pass can leave multi-MB answers in `<db>.broker.inbox.out/` past the TTL. That
is exactly the gap the architect's design position in `docs/reviews/architecture-exit-drain-6391.md`
(branch `item-6381`, rows **#6391/#6390**) asks the exit path to close: account for the spool
without touching the store.

**Residual.** `ui.mjs` has its own `quit` (`ui.mjs:315-316`) and headless `ui.mjs` exits 2 (needs a
TTY); `tui.mjs` registers no handler and is unmapped beyond `--help`. Whether `run --watch`'s own
clean drain should report 130 or 0 when it stops on a signal is a naming question the team can
close; today it reports 130 because the signal arrived while it was working.

## D263 — 2026-11-11T00:3xZ: **a bound is only real if the verb that took it can be PROVEN to take it — and a stop is not audited until the receipt is written on every leg that can notice it** (delegate rework after the completion audit rejected the first request; host measured with the measurement: **Linux**, **Fedora Linux 45 (Forty Five)**, kernel `7.2.15-300.fc45.x86_64`, node **v24.22.1**, `git version 2.56.0`)

**Status:** landed on `main` as `6cc13740` + this commit; nothing pushed.

**Context.** The audit of the first completion request measured the behavior on the live rig and still
rejected it on two grounds: (1) the record commit `c2c390e4` pushed `docs/NEXT.md` to 203 counted lines,
tripping `demo/next-pointer.test.mjs` and `demo/clockin-digest.test.mjs` (both assert the enforced 200-line
cap), so the gate the goal claimed ("294/294") was false against the delivered artifact; (2) the read path
was bounded but the spool-**mutating** verbs were not — `awaitIntentResult` (`cli.mjs:2007`) defaulted to
`timeoutMs = 15 * 60_000` and `pause --wait` (`cli.mjs:1982`) / `compactViaSpool` (`cli.mjs:1610`) called it
with no progress check. Separately, re-running the broker area found a #2322 hole the read drain's timing
exposed: `STOP-REQUESTED` is written at the top of the wake loop (`src/broker.mjs:1851`) and at the
`.stop`-file legs, but a signal noticed at the **idle** or **post-pass** leg set `stoppedBy="signal"` with
no receipt line — the audit logged `EXIT reason=signal` and nothing else.

**Decision.**
- **The mutating bound is derived, not configured.** `intentWaitBoundMs` (`src/broker.mjs:2422`) returns
  900,000 ms for an advancing broker (a compaction is real work), 10,000 ms for a degraded one (the same
  bound the read client uses), 0 when no broker is resident. It is re-read every poll, so a broker that
  recovers mid-wait is not cut off. The failure names pid, health, heartbeat age, pass age, live generation
  leases and `docs/runbooks/broker-down-or-stalled.md`; the intent stays in the spool.
- **The cap is met by archiving, not deleting.** The pinned-pi detail was moved **verbatim** to
  `docs/NEXT-ARCHIVE.md` (14,296 lines); `docs/NEXT.md` is 195 lines and keeps the heading plus the stop rule
  with a pointer into the archive.
- **Every leg that can notice a stop writes the receipt.** Both the idle leg and the post-pass leg now write
  `STOP-REQUESTED source=signal` when the stop came from a signal, so a signalled broker is never
  indistinguishable from a crash.

→ PASS 2.0 s (three legs: the pure bound, the live verb against a forged frozen broker, the advancing-broker
control that Ctrl-C still exits 130). `node demo/broker-stop-audit.test.mjs` → 0/12 red standalone, and the
`--area broker --jobs 4` loop that was **1/6 red** before the receipt fix is **0/6 red** after it. Live-rig bound,
read without pausing the fleet: `{boundMs: 10000, health: {state: "degraded", pid: 562329, hbAgeMs: 17863,
passAgeMs: 11209263}}`.

**Consequences.** A mutating verb now fails in the same shape as a read: fast, with a named cause and a
runbook, and never silently discarding the request. The general rule this goal established: **a bound you
cannot demonstrate with a mocked-plane demo is not a bound** — every bound added here got a `demo/` gate that
runs in under 5 s with no key and no network.


## D264 — (minted at land by the delegate landing pass; the branch carried it provisional per the ADR convention) store ownership is decided by process existence, never by heartbeat freshness (architect, item #6402, 2026-11-11)

**Decision:** the read path asks two separate questions and answers each with its own predicate:
`resident` = the OS says the broker pid exists (`ESRCH` semantics, the #3398 fail-safe), and
`progress` = `brokerHealth` (heartbeat leg plus `lastPassAt`). Routing is three-way — resident-and-advancing
→ spool with the long bound; resident-and-not-advancing → spool with a derived short bound, then a
structured refusal that carries the off-store state; proven-gone → local read. The write-mode store open
inside `readLocal` is gated on the pid being **proven gone**, not on heartbeat freshness and not on
generation-lease counts. `--local` is not an exception: it may take the read-only route while a pid exists.

**Context:** `src/readclient.mjs:246` routes to `readLocal` whenever `brokerAlive(state)` is false, and
`brokerAlive` includes a 60 s heartbeat gate (`src/broker.mjs:2352-2360`). A broker wedged inside a pass
lets its heartbeat age, so the exact condition the routing exists to survive is read as "no owner". The
write-mode fallback guard (`src/readclient.mjs:197`) asks whether a *seat* holds a generation lease — but
the store's owner is the broker process, and `openNodeSqliteStorage` migrates and wraps reads in
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. Measured with `tools/probes/routing-on-liveness-vs-progress.mjs`: a forged state naming
the probe's own live pid reports `pidAlive=true, brokerAliveFor=false`, and the read is served by opening
the store (`route=local`, 10.5 s).

**Alternatives considered:** (a) keep the lease gate and refresh the heartbeat — rejected, it treats the
symptom while the gate still answers the wrong question; (b) gate on process existence — chosen: cheap,
single predicate, reversible, and the read-only route remains available if it proves too strict;
(c) forbid all direct opens unless the broker is absent — rejected, a fresh rig has no broker and the
operator needs an escape hatch.

**Consequences:** some reads that today succeed will refuse — a wedged broker's store is unreadable until
it is stopped. Accepted: a second owner on a live owner is the `SessionFailed` corruption class, and the
refusal must carry what the operator actually needs (broker state, heartbeat age, pass age, spool counts,
lease counts) with store-derived sections labelled unavailable, so the diagnostic verb is not blinded by
the very condition it diagnoses. Every route must print which path served the read — the docstring at
`src/readclient.mjs:230` already claims this and the dead-pid path prints nothing (probe assertion I).

**Residual:** this decides the ownership gate and the bound shape. It does not decide which check-rule
finding the wedge should raise (`broker-state-pid-not-running` does not exist yet — probe assertion D),
nor whether a wedged broker should be self-healed by the supervisor; both are scope questions for `lead`.

## D275 — (provisional; re-mint at land from the MERGED tree — branches item-6664, item-6668 and this one have provisionally taken D272, D273 and D274; the number is minted at merge, never hardcoded) **row admission is a four-step order — existence, terminality, authority, applicability — and the verbs that collapse steps 2 and 4 are the ones that misreport a closed row as open work** (architect ruling on pm's row #6671, 2026-11-11)

**Status.** Design ruling on the amended build rows #6508-#6512 before they start. Sequencing is pm's; the helper is impl's; the verification leg is advocate's (#6670).

**Context.** DECISIONS.md already carries the rule from the #6185 ruling: "Terminality is checked before authority in every control verb." Measured with `node tools/probes/verb-admit-order-6671.mjs` (exit 1, real harness, real tools, faux turns, worktree HEAD `35001c3a`, pi-durable 1.3.0 from the lockfile): `defer_work`, `resume_work`, `hold_work`, `revise_work` and `cancel_work` all answer "not yours" for a `done` row they do not own; `release_work` is the only verb that follows the rule (`src/rig.mjs:1311` existence, `:1318` terminality #5778, `:1337` authority #6112, `:1339` applicability). `claim_work` by id answers three distinct situations — a terminal stranger's row, a live stranger's row, and my own held row — with the identical string `NO_QUEUED_WORK`. pm's amended #6510 reads "terminal, then status, then authority", which is not the order its own model verb uses: terminality and applicability are two different steps, and collapsing them makes the helper tell a stranger "the row is not held" when the operative fact is that they have no standing on it.

**Decision.** `admitRow(item, me, verb)` returns the first failing step in this order: **existence** (`unknown item #N`) → **terminality** (`already done/cancelled; nothing to <verb>`) → **authority** (`not a party`, with `release`'s scoped coordinator carve-out and its mandatory reason) → **applicability** (`is <status>; <verb> needs <expected>`). Every verb that touches a row calls it, and claim additionally calls `workable()` (D274): admission says *who may touch this row in this state*, workability says *is this row ready* — two questions, two functions, one call site each. Gate removal, when #6508 lands, follows the same authority shape: parties, or a coordinating seat carrying a reason, and it notifies the author the way cancellation does (#3470).

**Options considered.** (a) wire the six verbs and leave `claim_work` alone — rejected: claim is the leg the fleet uses hourly, and its failure is the one string the seat cannot act on. (b) keep per-verb ordering and document it — rejected on measurement: five of seven verbs already contradict the written rule, so a comment is not a control. (c) fold terminality and applicability into one "state" check, as the amended row reads — rejected because it re-creates the misreporting #5778 fixed: the reader learns the row's state instead of their own standing. Trade-off accepted: refusal text grows (id, reason, remedy), costing a little context per wake, in exchange for a refusal the seat can act on rather than escalate.

**Consequences.** Five verbs change the string they emit, so the #3663 `NAMES_ITS_VERB` goldens move in the same commit; the probe asserts the *class* of the refusal, not the wording, so the contract survives rewording. The helper must read status through the queue-lifecycle mapping pair (#3112 `effectiveStage`/`effectiveBlock`), or the ~30-literal migration (#3021) leaves it asserting literals. New observability requirement: coordinator standing is inferred from an ABSENT capability (`src/seattools.mjs:292-294`) — measured, the same seat and row flips from a refusal to a release when the seat declares nothing. A seat whose capabilities failed to register silently gains release authority; the reason requirement and the recorded transition are the current mitigation, and a check rule reporting "role implies work, capabilities empty" is the missing detector.

## D276 — (provisional; re-mint at land from the MERGED tree — D272-D275 are provisionally taken by branches item-6664, item-6668 and item-6671; the number is minted at merge, never hardcoded) **standing is stored data, never a capability string: authority comes from `from`/`to`/`block.resolver`, provisioning comes from a validated vocabulary, and a gate reference may reach one hop** (architect ruling on lead's #6673 / ruling #6672, 2026-11-11)

**Status.** Design ruling pinned before impl mints `gateStanding` (#6672). Verification leg is advocate's; the probe is in this branch.

**Context.** `src/seattools.mjs:262,292` answers two unrelated questions with one predicate: whether a seat needs working tools, and whether it may act on a row it did not mint. Measured with `node tools/probes/coordinator-standing-6673.mjs` (exit 1, real harness, HEAD `35001c3a`): `["design"]` → coordinator, 5 tools removed; `["review"]` → not; `[]` → coordinator. Through the verb (`src/rig.mjs:1315-1323`), a seat declaring only `["design"]` released a held row it is neither sender nor recipient of, while a seat declaring `["implement"]` was refused on the same kind of row. The census, counted as lead ruled: 12 seats declared, 2 coordinators by design (pm, lead), 3 seats carrying a capability string that confers nothing (`advocate`, `security`, `design`) — so no seat is mis-classified today, and the drift is one deletion away. On the gate side, `gateStanding` does not exist in `src/rig.mjs`: `normalizeBlockedBy` (`:391`) validates the shape of the list and `assertSendAllowed` (`:73-91`) checks the recipient's caps, but nothing checks who has the right to name an id. Measured: `designer` minted a row `blockedBy: [1]` on a row it has no part in — accepted.

**Decision.** Three separate instruments, never conflated.
1. **Authority** = stored fields: `item.from === seat || item.to === seat || item.block?.resolver === seat`, extended by mint-scoped reach (`#3470`). A gate reference is accepted only if the sender has standing on the target, or a row within ONE hop of the target's gate chain is a row the sender minted. Depth 2 is refused. The check runs at write — mint and `gate_work` — inside the commit, over the combined graph (#6512), never at read.
2. **Provisioning** = the seat's intersection with `WORKING_CAPABILITIES`, but the strings are validated at config load against `DECLARABLE_CAPABILITIES`. An undeclared capability is a config error, not a silent reclassification. `design` joins `WORKING_CAPABILITIES` with a recorded reason: design deliverables are commits (this branch's `docs/reviews/architecture-*.md` and probe files are the evidence). `route`, `plan`, `decide`, `adjudicate`, `advocate`, `security` stay declarable but non-working.
3. **The coordinator release carve-out stays**, but as a recorded lever rather than a derived classification, and the test that justifies delegating it remains reversibility: release is undoable by the sender, cancel and revise are not (D258 point 1).

**Options considered.** (a) keep derivation and add a `check` finding — rejected: a report that does not stop a write is not a control. (b) the three-instrument split above — chosen: cheap, data-driven, and reversible in one edit. (c) delete the coordinator release carve-out — rejected: a parked row whose gate is dead has no non-terminal repair for its parties (#3747, #6665), so removing it strands rows. Trade-off accepted: writes that succeed today will refuse, and refusals must name the target id, the seat's standing, and the legal alternative (mint the row carrying the gate, or ask a party) or the bound becomes an escalation generator.

**Consequences.** `gateStanding` must take `(seat, target, items)` and read only row fields — the probe asserts a non-party non-resolver is refused regardless of its capabilities, so an implementation that reads `seatIsCoordinator` cannot go green. Chains can only grow through parties, which is a behavioural narrowing for pm's routing habit of attaching gates to rows it merely observes: pm may still mint the row carrying the gate (D258 point 3). New observability requirement: `check` reports seats whose declared capabilities are all non-working, so pm and lead appear as an expected diff and any other seat appearing there is a fault. `requires` matching is string equality against caps (`src/rig.mjs:86-91`); once the vocabulary is closed, a `requires` value that matches nobody is impossible by construction rather than merely rare.

**Residual.** Whether load-time refusal (vs `check` reporting) is the right severity is lead's scope call. Cycle and dangling-id validation are #6497/#6512's, not this ruling's; this ruling only pins who may name an id and how far a reference may reach.
